WASHINGTON, DC – Last week, Congresswoman Hillary Scholten (D-MI-03), member of the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee, secured key policy victories and $115 million in authorized investments for West Michigan in the bipartisan Water Resources Development Act (WRDA) 2026 markup. The bill now moves from the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee to a vote on the full House floor.

“Updating and improving our water infrastructure keeps West Michigan communities safe and economically competitive,” said Congresswoman Scholten. “I’m proud of the policy wins and $115 million in new investments I’m advancing for our district, from shoreline protection in Muskegon Heights to protecting the health of the Great Lakes and improving dredging operations. I’ll keep working to get this bipartisan package across the finish line.”

Congresswoman Scholten’s specific wins include:

$115 million in new environmental infrastructure authorizations between Kent, Ottawa, and Muskegon Counties, as well as the state of Michigan, for water and wastewater infrastructure, including stormwater management and surface water resource protection.

The expedited completion of the streambank erosion and shoreline protection project in Muskegon Heights.

Language to direct the Army Corps to assess the impact of data centers on water resources.

The necessary authorization for a watershed-based study for the Muskegon River.

Several Great Lakes priorities, including language to adjust wage rates for Soo Locks employees; reauthorize the Great Lakes Commission; provide status updates on the Great Lakes recreational boating study; and expand funding eligibility to control aquatic plants and invasive species.

Dredging reforms to require local coordination and safe disposal of contaminated materials.

The reauthorization of FEMA’s High Hazard Potential Dam Program, and for language to assess levee risk, after significant flooding in Michigan this year.

text:
WASHINGTON – Today, U.S. Rep. Rashida Tlaib (MI-12) introduced the No AI Data Centers on Federal Lands Act, a new bill that permanently bans large AI data centers and associated infrastructure on land owned or managed by the U.S., including military bases. The bill also requires the removal of existing qualifying AI data centers and mandates site remediation.

“Everywhere I go in our district, our residents tell me loud and clear, data centers are not welcome in our communities. AI data centers bring noise, light, air, and water pollution, and can increase energy costs by as much as 267%,” said Rep. Tlaib, co-founder of the People’s Environmental Justice Caucus. “Our residents are choking on smog and already paying too much for their utility bills, yet the Trump administration wants to place heavier cost burdens on the shoulders of hardworking Americans. Our corrupt, AI-addicted President cannot be allowed to sacrifice our federal lands so that Big Tech oligarchs can get richer. I will continue to push back against harmful AI data centers alongside our residents to protect our public lands, health, and environment.”

In May, the Department of Defense requested $30 billion to build hyperscale data centers that would integrate largely untested hardware and software used to make life or death decisions into the military. These data centers could be built without Clean Air Act permits under the Trump administration’s new rule that revokes environmental protections. Recently, the Bureau of Land Management approved the first data center on BLM land in Nevada without public input, and the Department of Energy is pushing AI data centers at as many as 16 federal sites nationally. Tlaib’s bill would safeguard public lands from data center destruction, protect military families and surrounding neighborhoods from water and light pollution, and make it more difficult for the Trump administration to outsource military decisions to Big Tech companies.

The No AI Data Centers on Federal Lands Act is endorsed by the Center for Biological Diversity, Climate Justice Alliance, Food & Water Watch, and Win Without War. The bill is cosponsored by U.S. Rep. Jim McGovern (MA-02), Adelita Grijalva (AZ-07), Delia Ramirez (IL-03), Mark Pocan (WI-02), and Bonnie Watson Coleman (NJ-12).

“While the Trump administration willingly serves up our environment on a platter to Big Tech and their data centers, Rep. Tlaib’s proposed legislation is drawing a line in the sand,” said Camden Weber, senior climate and energy policy specialist at the Center for Biological Diversity. “Public lands belong to the people, not to Big Tech’s bottom line. This bill is a necessary step toward holding the industry accountable and protecting the air, water and places all species depend on.”

“Everyone deserves clean air, safe water, affordable energy, and healthy neighborhoods. But right now, the accelerated build out of AI data centers threatens this. Communities across the country are calling for accountability, not another giveaway for Big Tech,” Mar Zepeda Salazar, Legislative Director, Climate Justice Alliance. “The No AI Data Centers on Federal Lands Act establishes a critical guardrail to protect our public lands and ensures that the rush to build AI infrastructure does not come at the expense of our health, environment, or democratic voice. Communities have been clear: they deserve transparency, accountability, and the right to shape what gets built in their backyards.”

“With this legislation, Rep. Tlaib is showing the leadership required to protect public lands from massive data center development and industrial destruction,” said Jim Walsh, Food & Water Watch. “At a time when Big Tech is racing to build data centers across the country – including on sensitive public lands – communities are rising up to protect their air, water, health and financial security from this dangerous, exploitative industry.”

“Public lands should not be turned into sacrifice zones for the AI arms race,” said Shayna Lewis, Deputy Director of Win Without War. “This bill is a wake up call and a necessary safeguard that would protect communities from being forced to shoulder the energy, water, pollution, and infrastructure costs of systems designed to accelerate war-making and deepen the Pentagon’s deference to Big Tech.”

Today, Congresswoman Lori Trahan (D-MA-03) and Congressman Jay Obernolte (R-CA-23), alongside Representatives Scott Peters (D-CA-50), Scott Franklin (R-FL-18), Suhas Subramanyan (D-VA-10), and Erin Houchin (R-IN-09), introduced the Frontier Risk Oversight, National Transparency, Independent Evaluation, and Reporting (FRONTIER) Act. introduced the Frontier Risk Oversight, National Transparency, Independent Evaluation, and Reporting Act, or the FRONTIER Act. The bipartisan legislation, which was developed as part of the broader Great American AI Act framework, establishes a national, risk-based framework governing the development and deployment of the most advanced artificial intelligence models.

The FRONTIER Act establishes tiered requirements based on the size of a frontier AI developer, including model cards, risk-management frameworks, independent audits, incident reporting, and ongoing assessments. It also creates a uniform national standard for transparency, auditing, and reporting of catastrophic risk to prevent a patchwork of state regulations.

“As AI systems grow more capable, Americans deserve confidence that the most powerful models are being developed responsibly,” said Congresswoman Trahan. “The bipartisan FRONTIER Act delivers commonsense transparency and independent oversight for the largest AI developers while giving them a single, clear national standard to build on. This is how we protect the public from catastrophic risks without slowing the innovation that keeps America competitive.”

"Artificial intelligence is advancing rapidly, and Congress must ensure our regulatory framework keeps pace without undermining American innovation,” said Congressman Obernolte. “The FRONTIER Act focuses oversight on the largest developers and most advanced models, requiring transparency, independent evaluation, and timely reporting of serious safety incidents. This legislation will protect Americans from catastrophic risk, provide developers with clear rules of the road, and ensure the United States remains the global leader in AI.”

“The window to get AI policy right is closing, and Congress can't afford to miss it,” said Congressman Peters. “I supported Representatives Trahan and Obernolte's initial draft so we could develop a better bill that reflects how this technology works and where it's headed. Thanks to input from researchers, experts, and civil society advocates, that process worked. The FRONTIER Act is a targeted bill with clear, uniform transparency, and safety standards, instead of a fifty-state patchwork. I'm glad to support this bipartisan effort so that Congress acts before this technology outruns us.”

"The FRONTIER Act recognizes that not every AI developer should be regulated the same way. It takes a targeted approach by focusing only on the handful of companies developing the most powerful frontier AI models, not the startups and innovators driving America's AI ecosystem,” said Congressman Franklin. “By tying coverage to substantial AI research and development investments and requiring transparency and independent assessments from those developers, the bill avoids one-size-fits-all mandates and allows smaller innovators to spend their time building new technologies instead of navigating unnecessary federal red tape."

“This is a four-alarm fire. We need to take action now. These frontier models could have the power to create serious chaos and harm without adequate regulations. This bill, while not perfect, is an important, bipartisan step in the right direction. We need a bill like this that can actually pass this Congress and get signed into law. But this is only the first step, and more action needs to be taken to protect people from the harm these models can cause,” said Congressman Subramanyan.

"America must lead the world in artificial intelligence, and we can do that while being clear-eyed about the risks,” said Congresswoman Houchin. “Just this week, one of the most advanced AI systems in the country broke out of its own developer's testing environment, reaching systems it was never supposed to touch. This is exactly the kind of incident that shouldn't stay behind closed doors. The FRONTIER Act delivers transparency and accountability from the largest AI developers. Innovation and guardrails are not opposites—both are necessary to stay ahead of our adversaries."

Washington, D.C.-Rep. Van Epps (TN-07) participated in a Science, Space, and Technology (SST) Committee hearing titled, “Unleashing the Golden Age of Science: Examining the Priorities of the FY2027 Research and Technology Enterprise.”

Watch Rep. Van Epps' statement here.

Read Rep. Van Epps’ opening remarks here:

“Thank you, Director Kratsios, for being here today. In March 2025, President Trump charted out a clear vision for scientific progress and technological innovation: to position America to maintain leadership in emerging technologies like AI, quantum, and nuclear; to revitalize American scientific research; and to ensure that the growth of science and technology stimulates …economic growth.

Director Kratsios and OSTP have delivered by supporting these goals: the National AI Legislative Framework provided clear direction on how Congress should act to spur…on AI innovation that serves Americans, and an executive order signed by the President last month to accelerate U.S. innovation in quantum technologies to strengthen our national security.

One year after executive orders on nuclear energy, we are seeing real-world results. The President’s bold goal of three advanced test reactors achieving criticality before the Fourth of July was not only met but exceeded with four reactors achieving criticality. Just yesterday, Director Kratsios published a report establishing a blueprint for renewing American scientific leadership for the 21st century.

After the Biden administration floundered to position America for technology leadership and energy dominance, we are seeing tangible results from the Trump administration, with OSTP providing critical support.”

Read Rep. Van Epps’ questions here:

Rep. Van Epps asked, “ We must maintain the lead across the board when it comes to AI. Microsoft’s AI for Good Lab found that DeepSeek’s free, open-source models have driven AI adoption across the developing world. Recently, the Chinese company, Moonshot, released…a new open-weight model that performs competitively with American frontier models. US companies are turning toward open-source and open-weight models as they are cheaper, customizable, and… have less guardrails.

Just earlier this morning, the director of your team posted that Moonshot AI conducted large-scale covert distillation to develop their newest K3 model, and so a few questions here: How do we balance an open innovation ecosystem while protecting American technology from IP threat, and how is OSTP responding to the threat to American AI leadership posed by Chinese open source and open weight models?”

Director of White House Office of Science and Technology Policy, Michael Kratsios replied, “I think there's, for starters, an important distinction to be made between open source models and large scale industrial covert distillation of American models, and I think what was made public today was exactly that: the convert industrial distillation of…American technology. The administration deeply believes that the future of American leadership in AI is contingent upon having a…vibrant open and closed source set of models for Americans and the world to use. I think on the first or second page of the AI action plan the president released last year, we emphasized very strongly that the U.S. must lead in…open source. So for us, we're doing everything we can to…kind of push the open source community ahead in the U.S...and provide lots of alternatives for all of our entrepreneurs.

Rep. Van Epps asked, “Great, thanks, director. Modern research and AI model training runs on data, such as biological databases and materials data. American leadership in these fields depends on the quality and accessibility of that underlying data infrastructure. That's why I introduced the Web of Biological Data Act of 2026, which would establish a single point of entry for researchers to access high-quality biological data for use in research and development. Director, what…role does access to high-quality data play in America's science and AI ecosystem, and how would a single point of entry for standardized data sets impact the pace of innovation?

text:
Washington, D.C. – Today, Representatives George Whitesides (D-Calif.-27) and Bob Latta (R-Ohio-5) and U.S. Senators Adam Schiff (D-Calif.) and Jim Banks (R-Ind.) are introducing new bipartisan legislation to enhance the ability for AI labs and security researchers to combat distillation attacks from foreign adversaries and other frontier AI risks that pose a national security risk to the U.S.

The Collaboration on Adversarial Threats and Security Risks Act would allow for increased information sharing between industry and stakeholder groups to share information about AI security threats and coordinate their responses with other model developers. It includes strict guardrails, including protection against anti-competitive behavior, and permits the Attorney General to seek an injunction against non-Federal entities that abuse the exemption.

During distillation attacks, foreign labs systematically harvest data from U.S. AI models to produce their own advanced AI models at a fraction of the cost, posing an enormous threat to continued U.S. leadership and investment in developing the most powerful and efficient AI models and staying ahead of foreign competition. With the rise of AI, foreign labs have increasingly attacked proprietary models with millions of queries and use the resulting data to train rival, foreign-based systems, essentially reverse-engineering American technology at a lower cost and with less strain on valuable computational resources.

“As the Representative for a district at the heart of California’s aerospace and technology industry, I’ve seen firsthand how vital American innovation is to our national security. But as AI models grow exponentially more capable, the risk of these systems being exploited or weaponized poses a direct threat to public safety,” said Congressman Whitesides. “By authorizing threat intelligence sharing to defend against hostile foreign attacks, this bipartisan bill prevents our technology from being turned against us. Safeguarding our technological edge isn’t a partisan issue, and I’m proud to help lead this effort to keep America safe.”

“We cannot allow China, or any foreign adversary, to steal American technological advancements in AI, and then weaponize those advances to undermine our own national security,” said Senator Schiff. “The solution we are proposing would protect against AI distillation attacks and other security risks by allowing increased information-sharing among U.S. AI labs to counter the threat of foreign theft. As new AI innovations are developing faster than ever, it’s critical that Republicans and Democrats continue to work together to address potential misuse of AI development by hostile actors at home and abroad.”

“The AI race is one that America can’t afford to lose. Communist China is working every day to steal our technology and close the gap with the United States,” said Senator Banks. “American AI companies must be able to collaboratively defend against our adversaries. This bill gives them the tools to protect America’s technological edge and helps ensure we maintain our competitive edge.”

“Protecting the American people means ensuring the systems they rely on every day, including our hospitals, water systems, and electric grid, remain safe, secure, and reliable,” said Congressman Latta. “Our adversaries are constantly looking for new ways to target our critical infrastructure, and we must make sure we are prepared to respond. This bipartisan legislation, which I am proud to lead alongside Senators Schiff and Banks and Rep. Whitesides will help strengthen collaboration between American companies and ensure that when a threat is identified, we can quickly share information and take action to protect our communities. Our adversaries are working together to undermine us, and we must work together to defend America.”

Specifically, the Collaboration on Adversarial Threats and Security Risks Act would create a statutory exemption that allows non-Federal entities to:

Share information related to a covered AI security risk in good faith for the exclusive purpose of preventing, investigating, or mitigating an AI security risk; or

Coordinate with the exclusive purpose of reducing AI security risks by delaying or limiting the deployment of high-risk AI models, with required written notice prior to taking such actions.

The covered coordination efforts include information-sharing and agreements made through coordinating bodies such as the NSA’s AI Security Center, NIST’s CAISI, the Frontier Model Forum, or other industrial consortia. The legislation tracks the Cybersecurity Information Sharing Act, which has successfully enabled the sharing of cyber threat and vulnerability information between and among government and nongovernmental organizations for a decade.

In addition to Schiff, Banks, Latta, and Whitesides, the legislation is cosponsored by U.S. Representatives Pat Harrigan (R-N.C.-10), Darrell Issa (R-Calif.-48), Ted Lieu (D-Calif.-36), Mariannette Miller-Meeks (R-Iowa-01), Nathaniel Moran (R-Texas-01), and Jay Obernolte (R-Calif.-23).

The Collaboration on Adversarial Threats and Security Risks Act is endorsed by the AI Policy Network (AIPN), Alliance for a Better Future (ABF), Alliance for Secure AI, America First Policy Institute (AFPI), Association for Competitive Technology (ACT), Center for AI Safety (CAIS) Action Fund, Encode AI, Foundation for American Innovation (FAI) Action, Google, Health Information Sharing and Analysis Center (Health-ISAC), Law Reform Institute, SeedAI, and Software & Information Industry Association (SIIA).

“The worst AI security threats — a foreign adversary stealing a frontier model, a serious loss of control — won’t be contained to a single company. Developers need to be able to share threat information and coordinate, and this bill lets them do that. When companies can coordinate on threats without legal risk, they lose the excuse for staying silent and the public is safer for it,” said Sunny Gandhi, Co-Executive Director, Encode AI.

“We urgently need legislation that lets frontier AI developers collaborate on national security risks, such as adversarial distillation, without being deterred by uncertainties regarding antitrust law. The Collaboration on Adversarial Threats and AI Security Risks Act would provide targeted protections paired with appropriate guardrails against misuse,” said Tim Schnabel, President, Law Reform Institute.

“Building on the proven foundation of CISA 2015, The Collaboration on Adversarial Threats and Security Risks Act brings a strengthened threat-sharing framework into the AI era. Protecting critical infrastructure and cutting-edge AI systems requires real-time coordination against sophisticated security threats. This bill strikes a vital balance: empowering tech leaders to collaborate on cyber, CBRN, loss-of-control, and foreign adversarial risks while maintaining strong antitrust protections,” said Paul Lekas, Executive VP for Global Public Policy & Government Affairs, Software & Information Industry Association (SIIA).

“AI developers are confronting increasingly sophisticated threats involving model theft, unauthorized access, critical infrastructure, and other serious security risks. The Collaboration on Adversarial Threats and Security Risks Act would extend existing protections to information sharing and coordination around AI-specific threats, promoting real-time situational awareness among frontier labs and other AI developers. Importantly, the bill includes safeguards to ensure this protection is limited to good-faith security collaboration and does not excuse anticompetitive conduct,” said Morgan Reed, President, Association for Competitive Technology (ACT).

“The benefits of the CATS Act extend far beyond AI tech companies. By removing antitrust barriers to sharing critical information about adversarial AI threats, this legislation directly protects downstream critical infrastructure. For Health-ISAC and the health sector, this means safeguarding national public health and patient safety from emerging security risks and ultimately keeping Americans safer,” said Denise Anderson, President & CEO, Health-ISAC.

“Making America AI-ready means making institutions more resilient and equipped to respond to AI security risks. Giving companies a clear, lawful path to share threat information raises the security floor for the whole country while advancing American leadership in AI. Making America AI-ready means making institutions more resilient and equipped to respond to AI security risks. Giving companies a clear, lawful path to share threat information raises the security floor for the whole country while advancing American leadership in AI,” said Joshua New, Director of Policy, SeedAI.

“This bipartisan bill gives the AI industry clear rules of the road to share threat intelligence and collaborate on much-needed standards and benchmarks. We appreciate the leadership of Senators Schiff and Banks and Representatives Whitesides and Latta in working to ensure the continued responsible development of frontier models,” said John Connell, VP of Government Affairs and Public Policy, US & Canada, Google.

“I commend Senators Schiff and Banks for their bipartisan legislation. The Collaboration on Adversarial Threats and Strategic Risks Act improves the speed at which national security risks arising from adversarial espionage and autonomous improvement of artificial intelligence models can be identified and addressed,” said Mark Beall, President AI Policy Network.

“Advanced AI systems could be exploited by foreign adversaries, used to develop biological or cyber weapons, threaten critical infrastructure, or operate beyond meaningful human control. The Collaboration on Adversarial Threats and Security Risks Act is a commonsense step that will help America’s leading AI companies work together to identify and reduce these risks before they become an emergency,” said Brendan Steinhauser, CEO, The Alliance for Secure AI.

“As advanced AI systems increasingly become prime targets for espionage and theft by bad actors and global competitors, AI companies need a secure way to share threat information and coordinate defenses without risking antitrust violations. The Collaboration on Adversarial Threats and Security Risks Act would create a narrow exemption for companies to rely on, while keeping safeguards against price fixing, market allocation, and other anti-competitive behavior fully intact. By strengthening companies’ ability to detect and respond to these risks, this bill will help keep Americans protected from the real-world harms posed by compromised AI systems. The Center for AI Safety Action Fund is proud to support this bill,” said Varun Krovi, Executive Director, Center for AI Safety Action Fund.

WASHINGTON, D.C. – Today, Senators Jim Banks (R-Ind.) and Adam Schiff (D-Calif.) introduced the bipartisan Collaboration on Adversarial Threats and Security Risks Act, legislation to help American artificial intelligence companies work together to defend against espionage by Communist China and other serious national security threats.

As American companies race to advance Artificial Intelligence systems, foreign adversaries are increasingly attempting to steal U.S. technology through cyber-attacks, model theft, and ‘distillation’ attacks that replicate advanced AI models at a fraction of the cost. While existing laws allow companies to share information about cyber threats, there is no comparable legal framework allowing AI developers to coordinate against emerging AI-specific security risks.

The Collaboration on Adversarial Threats and Security Risks Act creates a narrowly tailored antitrust safe harbor allowing AI companies to share threat information and coordinate defensive measures in good faith to address defined national security risks while preserving existing antitrust protections against price-fixing, monopolization, and other anticompetitive conduct.

Sen. Jim Banks (R-Ind.): “The AI race is one that America can’t afford to lose. Communist China is working every day to steal our technology and close the gap with the United States. American AI companies must be able to collaboratively defend against our adversaries. The bill gives them the tools to protect America’s technological edge and helps ensure we maintain our competitive edge.”

Sen. Adam Schiff (D-Calif.): “We cannot allow China, or any foreign adversary, to steal American technological advancements in AI, and then weaponize those advances to undermine our own national security. The solution we are proposing would protect against AI distillation attacks and other security risks by allowing increased information-sharing among U.S. AI labs to counter the threat of foreign theft. As new AI innovations are developing faster than ever, it’s critical that Republicans and Democrats continue to work together to address potential misuse of AI development by hostile actors at home and abroad.”

Key Provisions of Collaboration on Adversarial Threats and Security Risks:

The legislation allows AI developers to collaborate to identify, assess, prevent, investigate, and mitigate defined AI security risks including:

Preventing the theft, distillation, weaponization, or misuse of advanced American AI models by foreign adversaries.

Sharing information on cybersecurity vulnerabilities, unauthorized access, and attacks targeting frontier AI systems.

Addressing AI-enabled chemical, biological, radiological, nuclear, and offensive cyber threats.

Coordinating responses to risks involving loss of operational control over advanced AI systems.

The legislation includes strict guardrails to ensure these protections cannot be used to undermine competition. It explicitly prohibits price-fixing, market allocation, monopolization, boycotts, or any other anticompetitive conduct unrelated to legitimate AI security and national security threats.

Background:

The legislation responds to growing evidence that foreign adversaries are conducting industrial-scale efforts to steal America’s most advanced AI capabilities. According to public reports, Chinese actors have used tens of thousands of fraudulent accounts to extract millions of interactions from leading U.S. AI systems in an effort to replicate frontier models. The White House has also warned that China is conducting deliberate campaigns to distill advanced American AI systems.

The bill has bipartisan, bicameral support and is supported by a broad coalition of organizations and experts.

“Building on the proven foundation of CISA 2015, the Collaboration on Adversarial Threats and Security Risks Act brings a strengthened threat-sharing framework into the AI era. Protecting critical infrastructure and cutting-edge AI systems requires real-time coordination against sophisticated security threats. This bill strikes a vital balance: empowering tech leaders to collaborate on cyber, CBRN, loss-of-control, and foreign adversarial risks while maintaining strong antitrust protections.” – Paul Lekas, Executive VP for Global Public Policy & Government Affairs, Software & Information Industry Association (SIIA).

“This bipartisan bill gives the AI industry clear rules of the road to share threat intelligence and collaborate on much-needed standard and benchmarks. We appreciate the leadership of Senators Schiff and Banks and Representatives Whiteside and Latta in working to ensure the continued responsible development of frontier models.” – John Connell, VP of Government Affairs and Public Policy, Google.

“The benefits of the CATS Act extend far beyond AI tech companies. By removing antitrust barriers to sharing critical information about adversarial AI threats, this legislation directly protects downstream critical infrastructure. For Health-ISAC and the health sector, this means safeguarding national public health and patient safety from emerging security risks and ultimately keeping Americans safer.” – Denise Anderson, President & CEO, Health-ISAC.

“Antitrust law was never meant to stop American AI companies from collaborating on security. This commonsense policy would give American AI developers the legal clarity they need to share threat intelligence and security best practices while preserving enforcement against genuine anticompetitive conduct. It’s a reform that strengthens American innovation and puts our national security first.” – Yusuf Mahmood, Policy Director, America First Policy Institute.

“Making America AI-ready means making institutions more resilient and equipped to respond to AI security risks. Giving companies a clear, lawful path to share threat information raises the security floor for the whole country while advancing American leadership in AI.” – Joshua New, Director of Policy, SeedAI.

“The worst AI security threats — a foreign adversary stealing a frontier model, a serious loss of control — won’t be contained to a single company. Developers need to be able to share threat information and coordinate, and this bill lets them do that. When companies can coordinate on threats without legal risk, they lose the excuse for staying silent, and the public is safer for it.” – Sunny Gandhi, Co-Executive Director, Encode AI.

“We urgently need legislation that lets frontier AI developers collaborate on national security risks, such as adversarial distillation, without being deterred by uncertainties regarding antitrust law. The Collaboration on Adversarial Threats and AI Security Risks Act would provide targeted protections paired with appropriate guardrails against misuse.” – Tim Schnabel, President, Law Reform Institute.

“AI developers are confronting increasingly sophisticated threats involving model theft, unauthorized access, critical infrastructure, and other serious security risks. The Collaboration on Adversarial Threats and Security Risks Act would extend existing protections to information sharing and coordination around AI-specific threats, promoting real-time situational awareness among frontier labs and other AI developers. Importantly, the bill includes safeguards to ensure this protection is limited to good-faith security collaboration and does not excuse anticompetitive conduct.” – Morgan Reed, President, Association for Competitive Technology (ACT).

“I commend Senators Schiff and Banks for their bipartisan legislation. The Collaboration on Adversarial Threats and Strategic Risks Act improves the speed at which national security risks arising from adversarial espionage and autonomous improvement of artificial intelligence models can be identified and addressed.” – Mark Beall, President, AI Policy Network.

“Advanced AI systems could be exploited by foreign adversaries, used to develop biological or cyber weapons, threaten critical infrastructure, or operate beyond meaningful human control. The Collaboration on Adversarial Threats and Security Risks Act is a common sense step that will help America’s leading AI companies work together to identify and reduce these risks before they become an emergency,” – Brendan Steinhauser, CEO, The Alliance for Secure AI.

“As advanced AI systems increasingly become prime targets for espionage and theft by bad actors and global competitors, AI companies need a secure way to share threat information and coordinate defenses without risking antitrust violations. The Collaboration on Adversarial Threats and Security Risks Act would create a narrow exemption for companies to rely on, while keeping safeguards against price fixing, market allocation, and other anti-competitive behavior fully intact. By strengthening companies’ ability to detect and respond to these risks, this bill will help keep Americans protected from the real-world harms posed by compromised AI systems. The Center for AI Safety Action Fund is proud to support this bill.” – Varun Krovi, Executive Director, Center for AI Safety Action Fund.

“America’s technology leadership is increasingly jeopardized by the inability of our frontier AI companies to coordinate on issues core to U.S. national security, from countering foreign espionage to cybersecurity information sharing. This bill provides the legal clarity needed for industry to collaborate on urgent AI security threats without undermining market competition.” – Samuel Hammond, Director of Artificial Intelligence & Chief Economist, the Foundation for American Innovation.

“As AI capabilities accelerate, so do the threats posed by foreign adversaries and malicious actors. Representative Latta’s bill removes unnecessary barriers to responsible collaboration, allowing companies to share critical security information in good faith to address covered AI risks. America’s AI leadership depends not only on innovation, but on ensuring our innovators can work together to defend the technologies that are essential to our economic and national security.” – Janet Kelly, CEO, Alliance for a Better Future.

“The Chinese Communist Party is actively seeking to close the AI gap through espionage and distillation of our most advanced AI models. American AI developers should not fear violating antitrust laws for collaborating to defend against those threats. This bill takes a commonsense step toward protecting U.S. technological leadership and preventing America’s most advanced AI systems from becoming tools of our adversaries.” – Autumn Dorsey, Center for Technology and the Human Person, The Heritage Foundation.

“The evidence is increasingly clear. AI companies in the U.S. are facing targeted attacks from PRC-aligned companies. Yet, existing antitrust law can discourage them from coordinating their defenses. A narrow, carefully tailored exemption would give responsible AI companies the confidence to share information and work together on serious threats without running afoul of competition law.” – Will Rinehart, Senior Fellow, AEI.

“Senator Banks’ Collaboration on Adversarial Threats and Securities Risks Act strikes the right balance between important AI security research collaboration and antitrust risk. While information sharing between rivals can create competition risk, the exemption in this bill is well crafted to minimize this concern while ensuring that AI labs are able to coordinate their defenses against our geopolitical adversaries.” – Gale Slater, Competition and Technology Policy Chair, American Compass.

text:
U.S. Senators Lisa Blunt Rochester (D-Del.) and Tim Sheehy (R-Mont.), both members of the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation, introduced the bipartisan Expanding AI Voices Act, which codifies and expands the National Science Foundation’s ExpandAI program to help more institutions build AI research capacity. The legislation will broaden the range of institutions and communities involved in AI research and workforce development, including first-generation college students, Minority-serving Institutions (MSIs), and rural colleges and universities. The House companion is led by Representatives Valerie Foushee (D-N.C.) and Zach Nunn (R-Iowa).

“AI offers tremendous opportunities for our communities and economies, but as this technology changes the way we live, we must guarantee that our students and our workforce still have the chance to succeed,” said Senator Blunt Rochester. “I’m proud to introduce the Expanding AI Voices Act alongside Senator Sheehy to ensure that no matter where we come from, we can all achieve our goals in the economy of the future.”

“America’s AI leadership depends on finding talent in every corner of the country. That’s why I’m introducing the Expanding AI Voices Act with Senator Blunt Rochester, which helps ensure students and researchers in Montana and other rural states have the opportunity to contribute to the future of AI innovation,” said Senator Tim Sheehy. “Our bipartisan legislation invests in people and institutions that have too often been overlooked, strengthens our workforce, and maintains America’s competitive edge by supporting critical innovation. Let’s get it done.”

The Expanding AI Voices Act would:

Expand AI research capacity by authorizing competitive NSF grants for emerging research institutions, including institutions outside the top 100 in federal R&D expenditures, Minority-Serving Institutions (MSIs), Historically Black Colleges and Universities (HBCUs), Tribal Colleges and Universities (TCUs), and eligible institutional consortia.

Expand AI research infrastructure by supporting access to advanced computing resources, high-speed networking, data facilities, and software engineering support needed to conduct cutting-edge AI research.

Build the AI workforce pipeline by supporting AI education, faculty recruitment and professional development, workforce training, and bridge programs that prepare students for graduate study and careers in artificial intelligence.

Accelerate AI innovation through partnerships by fostering collaboration among colleges and universities, nonprofit organizations, industry, Federal laboratories, state, local, and Tribal governments, and NSF AI Research Institutes.

Expand opportunity nationwide by encouraging geographic diversity, supporting institutions with limited AI research capacity, and increasing opportunities for students—including first-generation college students—to participate in AI research and education.

Promote safe, secure, and responsible AI by integrating safe, secure, and responsible AI practices and principles into AI education and workforce development programs.

Protect Taxpayer Dollars by requiring NSF to ensure awards complement—not duplicate—existing federal AI research programs.

“If we want to win the AI race, we can’t rely on a small handful of schools and people. SeedAI has experienced this first-hand during our AI Across America tour — it’s imperative that we go beyond the coasts and draw from the experiences and ingenuity of all Americans,” said Austin Carson, Founder and CEO of SeedAI. “The Expanding AI Voices Act will help build the AI research capacity needed to make that a reality. SeedAI thanks Senator Blunt Rochester and Senator Sheehy for their bipartisan leadership to strengthen American competitiveness.”

“America’s AI economy is moving faster than our workforce can keep up, and that gap will only widen without action. The Expanding AI Voices Act, introduced by Sens. Blunt Rochester (D-DE) and Sheehy (R-MT), meets that challenge head-on by giving students and teachers the tools to compete in an economy being reshaped by AI in real time. This bill also recognizes that opportunity shouldn’t be limited to those who can already afford a foothold. Its focus on first-generation undergraduate students ensures the next generation of AI talent includes voices from every background. BPC Action applauds Sens. Blunt Rochester and Sheehy for their leadership and urges the Senate to move quickly to pass it,” says Michele Stockwell, president, Bipartisan Policy Center Action.

“For America to lead on AI, we need to expand the pipeline of talent that’s fueling innovation,” said ARI President Brad Carson. “By investing in education, research, and workforce development across a broader range of institutions and communities, the Expanding AI Voices Act helps ensure the future of AI is shaped by the full scope of American talent. It’s exactly the kind of bipartisan, forward-looking policy the U.S. needs to maintain its edge in AI.”

The Expanding AI Voices Act is endorsed by the American Mathematical Society, Americans for Responsible Innovation, Association of Community College Trustees, Bipartisan Policy Center Action, Google, Leadership Conference on Civil and Human Rights, National Hispanic Health Foundation, SeedAI, Society of Hispanic Professional Engineers, IBM, Information Technology Industry Council (ITI), Thurgood Marshall College Fund.

text:
WASHINGTON — During a U.S. Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee oversight hearing of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC), U.S. Senator Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.), Ranking Member of the Committee, asked FERC Chairwoman Laura Swett and fellow Commissioners Lindsay See, Judy Chang, David LaCerte, and David Rosner, about how Congress can support incentivizing advanced transmission technologies and the potential to automize generator interconnection processes.

VIDEO: U.S. Senator Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.), Ranking Member of the Energy and Natural Resources Committee, questions FERC Commissioners during FERC Oversight Hearing, July 22, 2026.

On Incentives for Advanced Transmission Technologies:

Ranking Member Heinrich began his questioning by asking the Commissioners, “We all know that there haven't always been the built-in economic incentives to put some of those things onto the grid, despite the fact that they can often have very outsized and efficient impacts on how we utilize the existing grid in a way that doesn't require enormous economic upgrades. So I wanted to ask if you wanted to add anything to that conversation, and also what would be helpful from Congress in terms of congressional action to reinforce a posture of incentivizing these technologies? Commissioner See, do you want to jump on that first? You were the first to mention it.”

Commissioner See answered, “Happy to, Senator Heinrich. I think when we look at our reliability and affordability challenges, it's certainly necessary that we need to build new infrastructure, and that's expensive, so nobody's denying that. But there's also a really important moment for us to make the most out of the existing infrastructure, and that's when ATTs, GETs, these technologies can be incredibly helpful. They're not always the best solution, but they are, and they can give significant speed and cost savings to customers. I was really grateful that my colleagues and I were able to come together and include more language about that in the 206 orders we talked about to make sure that utilities take a hard look at these options when they're considering transmission upgrades. In terms of what more can be done, you know, FERC has limited authorities in this area, so we can encourage, we can incentivize. But if Congress, if this is an issue Congress wants to take up and gives FERC more clarity and authorities, I would love to see us to be able to run in this direction because I think it can be so helpful for both reliability and affordability.”

Heinrich followed, “Very helpful. Do either of you, the Chairwoman...”

Chairwoman Swett followed, “Thank you for the question, Senator. I fully agree with you and Commissioner See on this one. We're looking at GETs from every angle, and we recently had a software conference where I had a panel added to have... panelists specifically who have experience implementing GETs in their utilities and their markets to see how that's playing out, the economics associated with it, and I think it's getting a lot of traction. The biggest barrier, to answer your question at a point, the Federal Power Act prohibits FERC explicitly from mandating building of any particular transmission facility, except for the backstop siting authority, and it is my personal opinion as a lawyer that GETs fall under that category. So until Congress changes that prohibition, FERC’s not really able to instruct anything more aggressively.”

Heinrich followed, “But you can force the analysis, which can then show the most efficient economic path.”

Swett followed, “And we have required that type of analysis in our June orders.

Heinrich followed, “Commissioner Chang?”

Chang answered, “Great, thank you very much, Senator, for that question. I too support the use of advanced transmission technology more than support. I think it's time that we take pilot projects and the industry takes pilot projects and really implement the most advanced technologies to save consumers’ money. Again, if the U.S. wants to be a leader in technology, this is another set of technology that we can lead in the industry. When it comes to, certainly, I think if Congress wants to work on this, we would be very happy to implement any particular changes under the current authority when transmission owners and developers come to FERC and request for incentives. I think there is some room for FERC to ask the transmission owners and developers to demonstrate to and illustrate, or to explain what technologies they're implementing and what else they have considered and why they are not adopting the best technologies.”

Heinrich answered, “I appreciate that.”

On Generator Interconnection Process Reform and AI:

Heinrich asked, “According to Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, at the end of 2025, there were more than 8,200 proposed power plants trying to connect to the grid, but only 13% of the capacity that has attempted to get on the grid between 2000 and 2020 has actually reached commercial operation. I recently introduced the Grid Connection and Congestion Management Act, which would allow generators to interconnect even faster to the grid. But I want to ask you, Commissioner Rosner, what steps beyond Order 2023 should FERC take to further improve generator interconnection processes? In particular, you mentioned automation and AI tools, and I think that's a space that we're just beginning to see the potential of. And if so, if you could touch on that, I would appreciate it.”

Commissioner Rosner responded, “Thank you for the question, Senator Heinrich, and yes, I think it's obvious to me that there's a huge opportunity to be smarter about how we run our interconnection processes. The Texas model is one example. Implementing automation on our current queue cluster study process is another example. In the SPP region (Southwest Power Pool) region, we had a proposal from them that they brought to us with unanimous support from their states that reimagined how to do both generator interconnection and transmission planning together. But back on automation, there's a huge opportunity there in MISO. Their old way with pen and paper and engineers doing the power flow studies, it took them 686 days to process their 2021 cluster, over 100 gigawatts of generation. Using automation, the new way—less than 10 days. And there's open public benchmarking on how well this worked. It was very, very close and continues to get better. And from my perspective, this is all about, let's give applicants, people who want to connect new power plants to the grid, let's give them the answer on whether it makes sense to connect to the grid in that location or not. And also, I wouldn't be doing my job if I didn't already say appreciate your leadership on transmission, regional, interregional. None of these interconnection queue reforms work if there isn't a grid to plug the power plant into, and we can talk more about some examples of how that hasn't worked so well recently, and that's a huge problem.”

A video of Heinrich's questioning can be found here.

“Ohio is the best state in the nation to start and grow a business, and this bill will give more entrepreneurs a path to success.”

WASHINGTON – Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio) joined Sens. James Lankford (R-Okla.) and Chris Coons’ (D-Del.) in introducing the bipartisan New Opportunities for Business Ownership and Self-Sufficiency (NO BOSS) Act to support individuals as they pursue small business ownership.

The bill would strengthen the underutilized Self-Employment Assistance (SEA) Program by reducing barriers for states to participate and encouraging broader use of the program.

“Ohio is home to more than 1.1 million small businesses, and they are the backbone of our state’s economy. This legislation will help more Americans achieve the dream of owning a small business by creating a stronger pathway from unemployment to self-employment. Ohio is the best state in the nation to start and grow a business, and this bill will give more entrepreneurs a path to success,” said Husted.

“If you lose your job, the government shouldn’t tell you the only way forward is to go work for somebody else. Some folks have a business idea they’ve been dreaming about for years, and losing a job might be the push to finally chase it. Right now, an outdated federal rule forces people on unemployment to spend their time applying for jobs they don’t want instead of building the business they do want. Our bill fixes that. If you’re willing to put in the work to start a business, hire your neighbors, and build something in your community, we should cheer you on, not stand in your way,” said Lankford.

“Every small business began with someone taking a chance on a new idea, and new AI tools will make it easier than ever to turn those ideas into business plans, sales, and storefronts. Americans shouldn’t have to choose between the safety net of unemployment benefits that they’ve paid into and the all-American opportunity to chase their entrepreneurial dream. As artificial intelligence reshapes the nature of work, this bill will help support American entrepreneurs, keep food on families’ tables, lift up small businesses, and keep our economy strong,” said Coons.

Reps. Mike Carey (R-Ohio) and Greg Landsman (D-Ohio) are leading the companion version of the No BOSS Act in the U.S. House of Representatives. The No BOSS Act passed the House unanimously on April 29, 2026.

“Small businesses and pioneering entrepreneurs are the engine of our economy, but making the leap from unemployment to self-employment is risky. Americans shouldn’t be forced to choose between unemployment insurance and working on their next big idea. This bill makes it easier to start and sustain a small business, and I am proud to once again lead this effort,” said Carey.

“This is a real unique opportunity to help unemployed individuals start a business with dignity. By making commonsense changes to the program, we can empower entrepreneurship and give people who are passionate about building a business the support they need to make it a reality,” said Landsman.

Background:

The SEA Program is designed to encourage unemployed individuals to start their own businesses. Unlike traditional Unemployment Compensation (UC), SEA participants can utilize weekly payments towards getting their small business off the ground.

Only five states have active SEA programs for UC claimants as of 2025 (Delaware, Mississippi, New Hampshire, New York and Oregon). As of 2022, Oregon and New York had the largest SEA programs with 390 and 1,005 participants, respectively.

The NO BOSS Act would improve use of the SEA program by making common-sense changes to the program, many modeled after the program’s highly successful implementation in Oregon.

The bill would remove the “likely to exhaust benefits” provision, which prevents many unemployed workers from participating in this program and implies that entrepreneurship should only be for those who are unlikely to find any other job.

Additionally, the legislation would clarify that a state-approved business plan and market feasibility study could serve as an alternative requirement to entrepreneurship training.

This builds on Husted’s work to support small businesses. In the Senate, Husted is supporting the:

Made in America Manufacturing Financing Act: This bill would expand access to growth capital for small U.S.-based manufacturers.

Investing in All of America Act: This bill would expand access to capital for small businesses in rural and low-income communities, as well as those in the manufacturing and critical technology sectors.

AI for Mainstreet Act: This bill would provide training, guidance and support to American small businesses looking to implement AI into their businesses.

Repealing Big Brother Overreach Act: This bill would eliminate the requirement for small businesses to report beneficial ownership information to the Treasury Department, which is burdensome and overreaching.

text:
Watch in NBC: Sen. Mark Kelly says the U.S. government should be ‘more proactive’ about AI scams

Today, Senators Mark Kelly (D-AZ) and Jim Justice (R-WV) introduced the Senior Chatbot Protection Act to keep older Americans safe by requiring AI chatbot and voice assistant companies to provide clear disclosures, safeguard sensitive conversations, and end deceptive design practices in their products.

The legislation expands on Kelly’s ongoing efforts to ensure AI works for all Americans, including seniors. In June, Kelly introduced the bipartisan Aging with AI Act, which would research how AI tools impact older Americans.

Last year, Kelly called on the Senate Special Committee on Aging to hold a hearing on the issue. The hearing will be held next week.

“AI is a powerful tool that can help seniors live more independently. It can help them manage their finances, keep track of medications and doctor’s appointments, and navigate everyday tasks that become more challenging with age,” saidKelly. “But seniors need to know when they’re talking to a machine, what its limits are, and how their information is being used to make sure they aren’t being scammed or put at risk.”

“A.I. chatbots are an incredible tool for older Americans, but we can’t miss the opportunity to protect our seniors who rely on chatbots for support, companionship, and even important decisions during critical times. The Senior Chatbot Protection Act sets transparency standards so our seniors know they are speaking with a chatbot and not a real person—whether in everyday conversations or when making high-stakes decisions. I applaud Senator Kelly for spearheading this important legislation that can make a real difference in the lives of our seniors,” said Justice.

In May, the FBI reported that Americans over 60 years old submitted more than 201,000 internet-crime complaints and reported more than $7.7 billion in losses in 2025. Reuters recently covered the story of a cognitively impaired 76-year-old New Jersey man who died while traveling to meet a woman he believed was real but was actually a Meta AI chatbot.

Background:

The Senior Chatbot Protection Act ensures that transparency and safeguards support user autonomy while strengthening—not replacing—human judgment and trusted relationships. The bill would protect older Americans by:

Requiring clear AI disclosures so that users would be told when they are interacting with AI, and companies could not falsely represent that a chatbot is human or that a response came from a licensed professional.

Providing added protections when a conversation involves health care, estate planning, guardianship, or a crisis so that the chatbot would provide additional warnings, direct users toward appropriate support, and make clear it is not a substitute for qualified professional advice.

Protecting sensitive conversations by making companies face limits on using covered conversation data for targeted advertising, profiling, sharing with third parties, or AI training without clear consent. Users would have a clear way to delete conversation history.

Addressing deceptive design practices by ensuring companies take steps to prevent designs that encourage excessive reliance, discourage users from seeking help from family or professionals, or pressure users to keep engaging after they try to stop.

The bill also directs the National Institute of Standards and Technology to develop voluntary guidance for AI chatbots interacting with older adults, covering transparency, usability, crisis response, fraud and scam prevention, and privacy.

text:
Senator Marshall Delivers Remarks in Support of the Protecting American Taxpayers Act

Washington – On Wednesday, U.S. Senator Roger Marshall, M.D. (R-Kansas), delivered remarks on the Senate floor calling on his colleagues to end the era of no accountability and fraud by passing the Protecting American Taxpayers Act.

Senator Marshall emphasized this bill is projected to save $240 billion in taxpayer funds, which would otherwise go to thieves and fraudsters, and he called on members of both parties to come together with the common goal of putting the American taxpayer first.

Click HERE to download the full video.

Senator Marshall’s full speech as delivered:

“Mr. President, just two years ago, we were a land of open borders. Crime was surging across the country, and fraud was rampant. But today — today the borders are secure, crime and murder rates are at a 100-year low, and fraudsters are going to jail. And that’s why today I’m rising to support the Protecting American Taxpayers Act.”

“For years, Washington accepted fraud as the cost of doing business. The government wrote the checks, the fraudsters cashed them, and hardworking Americans were left to foot the bill. And those same hardworking Americans knew intuitively that that was driving up their cost of living. But those days are coming to an end.”

“Under President Trump, we’ve seen historic momentum to root out waste, fraud, and abuse across the federal government. For the first time in a long time, Washington is shining a flashlight on the billions of taxpayer dollars disappearing through fraud, improper payments, and outright criminal activity. Now, Congress has a responsibility to finish the job.”

“The American people are asking a simple question: ‘If Washington knows where the fraud is, why aren’t we stopping it?’ And they’re right to ask. Today, an estimated $1.4 billion is stolen from taxpayers every single day. That’s money that should be strengthening our military, supporting our veterans, protecting Medicare and Social Security, or reducing the debt we’re leaving to our children and our grandchildren. Instead, it’s ending up in the hands of organized fraud rings, scam artists, and criminals who have learned exactly where the holes in our federal government are.”

“We’re already seeing what happens when the federal government makes fraud enforcement a priority. In one of the largest healthcare fraud takedowns in our nation’s history, federal prosecutors charged hundreds of defendants accused of submitting more than $6 billion in fraudulent claims to Medicare, Medicaid, and other taxpayer-funded health programs. And the best part: people are finally going to jail.”

“Investigators uncovered transnational criminal organizations, fraudulent medical equipment schemes, and providers accused of billing the government for services that were never provided. These weren’t bookkeeping mistakes; they were sophisticated efforts to steal billions from the American taxpayer.”

“Now the truth is simple — fraudsters follow the money, and for too long Washington has rolled out the welcome mat. This legislation finally starts closing that door. The Protecting American Taxpayers Act is projected to save taxpayers $240 billion — that’s $240 billion — by preventing fraud before it happens, recovering stolen taxpayer dollars, and ensuring criminals are held accountable. It doesn’t just respond to fraud after the fact — it helps stop it before another billion dollars walks out the door.”

“One piece of this package that I’m proud to see included is my WALZ Act. W-A-L-Z, the WALZ Act. Named after — you guessed it — a certain governor who allowed fraud to run rampant in his state. The idea behind it is about as simple as it gets — don’t pay first and ask questions later. Kansas families don’t do business that way, and small businesses don’t do business that way. If you’re remodeling your kitchen, you don’t hand the contractor every penny before a single cabinet’s installed. If you’re hiring someone to fix your roof, you don’t write the check before the work’s finished — you pay after the job is done.”

“Yet that’s exactly the opposite of how Washington has too often operated. For years, the federal government has pushed billions of dollars out the door up front with little accountability, then acted surprised when criminals disappeared with the money. My WALZ Act simply says federal payments should be made as reimbursements after the services have actually been provided. That one simple reform closes one of the biggest loopholes that’s allowed billions of taxpayer dollars to be stolen before they ever get the chance to disappear.”

“But this package doesn’t stop there — it claws back unused COVID funds, strengthens the Treasury’s fraud detection systems, extends the statute of limitations so pandemic fraudsters can’t simply run out the clock, it protects our veterans from scammers, it combats emerging AI-generated fraud, and gives law enforcement stronger tools to hold criminals accountable. Taken together, these reforms represent one of the strongest anti-fraud packages Congress has considered in years.”

“Now, my colleagues on the other side of the aisle spend years responding to every problem the same way — throwing more money at it. We believe the first question should be, ‘Where is the fraud? Where is the waste? Where is the abuse? And how do we stop it before asking taxpayers for another dime?’”

“This administration has created real momentum. For the first time in years, we’re not just talking about fraud — we’re finding it, prosecuting it, and putting criminals on notice that stealing from the American taxpayer has consequences. People are already being held accountable, and more need to be. Congress should build on that momentum by giving law enforcement and federal agencies the tools they need to keep fraudsters out of our programs and behind bars where they belong.”

“So, let’s not waste this opportunity — let’s make these reforms permanent, let’s close the loopholes once and for all, let’s protect the taxpayers who fund the government, and let’s send a clear message that the era of easy money for fraudsters is over. I urge every one of our colleagues to support the Protecting American Taxpayers Act. Thank you, Mr. President, and I yield the floor.”

text:
Washington, D.C. – Today, U.S. Senators Adam Schiff (D-Calif.) and Jim Banks (R-Ind.), and Representatives Bob Latta (R-Ohio-5) and George Whitesides (D-Calif.-27) are introducing new bipartisan legislation to enhance the ability for AI labs and security researchers to combat distillation attacks from foreign adversaries and other frontier AI risks that pose a national security risk to the U.S.

The Collaboration on Adversarial Threats and Security Risks Act would allow for increased information sharing between industry and stakeholder groups to share information about AI security threats and coordinate their responses with other model developers. It includes strict guardrails, including protection against anti-competitive behavior, and permits the Attorney General to seek an injunction against non-Federal entities that abuse the exemption.

During distillation attacks, foreign labs systematically harvest data from U.S. AI models to produce their own advanced AI models at a fraction of the cost, posing an enormous threat to continued U.S. leadership and investment in developing the most powerful and efficient AI models and staying ahead of foreign competition. With the rise of AI, foreign labs have increasingly attacked proprietary models with millions of queries and use the resulting data to train rival, foreign-based systems, essentially reverse-engineering American technology at a lower cost and with less strain on valuable computational resources.

“We cannot allow China, or any foreign adversary, to steal American technological advancements in AI, and then weaponize those advances to undermine our own national security,” said Senator Schiff. “The solution we are proposing would protect against AI distillation attacks and other security risks by allowing increased information-sharing among U.S. AI labs to counter the threat of foreign theft. As new AI innovations are developing faster than ever, it’s critical that Republicans and Democrats continue to work together to address potential misuse of AI development by hostile actors at home and abroad.”

“The AI race is one that America can’t afford to lose. Communist China is working every day to steal our technology and close the gap with the United States,” said Senator Banks. “American AI companies must be able to collaboratively defend against our adversaries. This bill gives them the tools to protect America’s technological edge and helps ensure we maintain our competitive edge.”

“Protecting the American people means ensuring the systems they rely on every day, including our hospitals, water systems, and electric grid, remain safe, secure, and reliable,” said Congressman Latta. “Our adversaries are constantly looking for new ways to target our critical infrastructure, and we must make sure we are prepared to respond. This bipartisan legislation, which I am proud to lead alongside Senators Schiff and Banks and Rep. Whitesides will help strengthen collaboration between American companies and ensure that when a threat is identified, we can quickly share information and take action to protect our communities. Our adversaries are working together to undermine us, and we must work together to defend America.”

“As the Representative for a district at the heart of California’s aerospace and technology industry, I’ve seen firsthand how vital American innovation is to our national security. But as AI models grow exponentially more capable, the risk of these systems being exploited or weaponized poses a direct threat to public safety,” said Congressman Whitesides. “By authorizing threat intelligence sharing to defend against hostile foreign attacks, this bipartisan bill prevents our technology from being turned against us. Safeguarding our technological edge isn’t a partisan issue, and I’m proud to help lead this effort to keep America safe.”

Specifically, the Collaboration on Adversarial Threats and Security Risks Act would create a statutory exemption that allows non-Federal entities to:

Share information related to a covered AI security risk in good faith for the exclusive purpose of preventing, investigating, or mitigating an AI security risk; or

Coordinate with the exclusive purpose of reducing AI security risks by delaying or limiting the deployment of high-risk AI models, with required written notice prior to taking such actions.

The covered coordination efforts include information-sharing and agreements made through coordinating bodies such as the NSA’s AI Security Center, NIST’s CAISI, the Frontier Model Forum, or other industrial consortia. The legislation tracks the Cybersecurity Information Sharing Act, which has successfully enabled the sharing of cyber threat and vulnerability information between and among government and nongovernmental organizations for a decade.

In addition to Schiff, Banks, Latta, and Whitesides, the legislation is cosponsored by U.S. Representatives Pat Harrigan (R-N.C.-10), Darrell Issa (R-Calif.-48), Ted Lieu (D-Calif.-36), Mariannette Miller-Meeks (R-Iowa-01), Nathaniel Moran (R-Texas-01), Lori Trahan (D-Mass.-03), and Jay Obernolte (R-Calif.-23).

The Collaboration on Adversarial Threats and Security Risks Act is endorsed by the AI Policy Network (AIPN), Alliance for a Better Future (ABF), Alliance for Secure AI, America First Policy Institute (AFPI), Association for Competitive Technology (ACT), Center for AI Safety (CAIS) Action Fund, Encode AI, Foundation for American Innovation (FAI) Action, Future of Life Institute, Google, Health Information Sharing and Analysis Center (Health-ISAC), Law Reform Institute, SeedAI, and Software & Information Industry Association (SIIA).

“The worst AI security threats — a foreign adversary stealing a frontier model, a serious loss of control — won’t be contained to a single company. Developers need to be able to share threat information and coordinate, and this bill lets them do that. When companies can coordinate on threats without legal risk, they lose the excuse for staying silent and the public is safer for it,” said Sunny Gandhi, Co-Executive Director, Encode AI.

“We urgently need legislation that lets frontier AI developers collaborate on national security risks, such as adversarial distillation, without being deterred by uncertainties regarding antitrust law. The Collaboration on Adversarial Threats and AI Security Risks Act would provide targeted protections paired with appropriate guardrails against misuse,” said Tim Schnabel, President, Law Reform Institute.

“Building on the proven foundation of CISA 2015, The Collaboration on Adversarial Threats and Security Risks Act brings a strengthened threat-sharing framework into the AI era. Protecting critical infrastructure and cutting-edge AI systems requires real-time coordination against sophisticated security threats. This bill strikes a vital balance: empowering tech leaders to collaborate on cyber, CBRN, loss-of-control, and foreign adversarial risks while maintaining strong antitrust protections,” said Paul Lekas, Executive VP for Global Public Policy & Government Affairs, Software & Information Industry Association (SIIA).

“AI developers are confronting increasingly sophisticated threats involving model theft, unauthorized access, critical infrastructure, and other serious security risks. The Collaboration on Adversarial Threats and Security Risks Act would extend existing protections to information sharing and coordination around AI-specific threats, promoting real-time situational awareness among frontier labs and other AI developers. Importantly, the bill includes safeguards to ensure this protection is limited to good-faith security collaboration and does not excuse anticompetitive conduct,” said Morgan Reed, President, Association for Competitive Technology (ACT).

“The benefits of the CATS Act extend far beyond AI tech companies. By removing antitrust barriers to sharing critical information about adversarial AI threats, this legislation directly protects downstream critical infrastructure. For Health-ISAC and the health sector, this means safeguarding national public health and patient safety from emerging security risks and ultimately keeping Americans safer,” said Denise Anderson, President & CEO, Health-ISAC.

“Making America AI-ready means making institutions more resilient and equipped to respond to AI security risks. Giving companies a clear, lawful path to share threat information raises the security floor for the whole country while advancing American leadership in AI. Making America AI-ready means making institutions more resilient and equipped to respond to AI security risks. Giving companies a clear, lawful path to share threat information raises the security floor for the whole country while advancing American leadership in AI,” said Joshua New, Director of Policy, SeedAI.

“This bipartisan bill gives the AI industry clear rules of the road to share threat intelligence and collaborate on much-needed standards and benchmarks. We appreciate the leadership of Senators Schiff and Banks and Representatives Whitesides and Latta in working to ensure the continued responsible development of frontier models,” said John Connell, VP of Government Affairs and Public Policy, US & Canada, Google.

“I commend Senators Schiff and Banks for their bipartisan legislation. The Collaboration on Adversarial Threats and Strategic Risks Act improves the speed at which national security risks arising from adversarial espionage and autonomous improvement of artificial intelligence models can be identified and addressed,” said Mark Beall, President AI Policy Network.

“Advanced AI systems could be exploited by foreign adversaries, used to develop biological or cyber weapons, threaten critical infrastructure, or operate beyond meaningful human control. The Collaboration on Adversarial Threats and Security Risks Act is a commonsense step that will help America’s leading AI companies work together to identify and reduce these risks before they become an emergency,” said Brendan Steinhauser, CEO, The Alliance for Secure AI.

“As advanced AI systems increasingly become prime targets for espionage and theft by bad actors and global competitors, AI companies need a secure way to share threat information and coordinate defenses without risking antitrust violations. The Collaboration on Adversarial Threats and Security Risks Act would create a narrow exemption for companies to rely on, while keeping safeguards against price fixing, market allocation, and other anti-competitive behavior fully intact. By strengthening companies’ ability to detect and respond to these risks, this bill will help keep Americans protected from the real-world harms posed by compromised AI systems. The Center for AI Safety Action Fund is proud to support this bill,” said Varun Krovi, Executive Director, Center for AI Safety Action Fund.

The full text of the legislation is available here.

A one pager on the legislation is available here.
