Washington, D.C. — U.S. Representative Sean Casten (IL-06) led 17 House Democrats in a letter to Department of Energy Secretary Chris Wright scrutinizing DOE’s decision to award $18.5 million for the construction of a new coal plant to a QAnon conspiracy theorist with no relevant experience.

“We are especially concerned about the apparent lack of due diligence conducted by your Department regarding this project. The purpose of the LPO is to provide funding to energy projects that will meaningfully lower costs for all Americans, but only after rigorously evaluating the economic and technical viability of the projects and regardless of any political agenda or intention to advance a favored technology,” the lawmakers wrote. “...The last coal plant in the U.S. was constructed in 2013. Older coal-fired power plants incur higher operating and maintenance costs, making it more expensive to operate existing plants than transition to cleaner, renewable sources.”

The lawmakers also noted the award applicant's lack of experience in the energy industry. Notably, the award applicant holds political ties to the president.

“We raise these concerns in light of the applicant Alex Phillips's lack of relevant experience, his political ties to the President, and the fundamental economic unsoundness of the proposal,” the lawmakers continued. “The decision to award funds to a political ally for a utility-scale generation project represents a major step backward for the stability and affordability of our electric grid and sets a dangerous precedent for more politically influenced deals that will jeopardize progress towards building an electric grid that supports a thriving U.S. economy.”

In addition to Rep. Casten, the letter was signed by Reps. Bonamici, Quigley, Khanna, Levin, Matsui, Mullin, Deluzio, McCollum, Ansari, Jonathan Jackson, Foushee, Pingree, Ross, DeGette, Trahan, Krishnamoorthi, and Beyer.

Text of the letter can be found below. A copy of the letter can be found here.

Dear Secretary Wright:

We write to express our concerns regarding the $18.5 million loan awarded by the Energy Department’s Loan Programs Office (LPO) to TerraSpark, an “eco-friendly” energy developer, for the construction of a new coal- burning plant. We are especially concerned about the apparent lack of due diligence conducted by your Department regarding this project. The purpose of the LPO is to provide funding to energy projects that will meaningfully lower costs for all Americans, but only after rigorously evaluating the economic and technical viability of the projects and regardless of any political agenda or intention to advance a favored technology.

We raise these concerns in light of the applicant Alex Phillips's lack of relevant experience, his political ties to the President, and the fundamental economic unsoundness of the proposal. The decision to award funds to a political ally for a utility-scale generation project represents a major step backward for the stability and affordability of our electric grid and sets a dangerous precedent for more politically influenced deals that will jeopardize progress towards building an electric grid that supports a thriving U.S. economy.

We write as well in the belief that the hard-working people of West Virginia do not need more false promises. The last coal plant in the U.S. was constructed in 2013. Older coal-fired power plants incur higher operating and maintenance costs, making it more expensive to operate existing plants than transition to cleaner, renewable sources. Since 2021, the cost to operate a coal plant has increased by 28%. Almost one quarter of active coal power plants are slated for retirement by 2029.

Residents of West Virginia in particular have seen a 34% increase in utility bills from 2019 to 2024. Three of the active coal plants under Appalachian Power, accounting for 87% of West Virginia’s electricity, lost a combined $81 million in 2025. Overreliance on expensive coal generation significantly contributes to rising utility costs and lack of economic growth in the region. Meanwhile, onshore wind and utility-scale solar costs have dropped 90%. The myth that coal power energy is better or cheaper helps no one – not the energy consumer, not the taxpayer, and certainly not hard-working people ready for a future in a modern energy economy.

Additional elements of the TerraSpark proposal raise further concerns. The inclusion of a 1 gigawatt artificial intelligence (AI) data center requires significant technical and managerial expertise to ensure electricity demand can be properly met. Also, TerraSpark claims to have an unconventional approach to carbon capture that differentiates it from other coal companies on the market, a chilling assertion given the rarity of a successful power plant/carbon capture combination. It will be essential to examine this technology with rigorous scrutiny to ensure emission reduction targets are met without any harmful impacts on the surrounding community and environment.

In order to confirm that your Department conducted appropriate due diligence, we respectfully request submission of the following information by September 1, 2026:

The biographies of the principals, key project leads, and partners of TerraSpark and any contractors or subcontractors on this project, including relevant experience in building similar projects.

Any application fee collected related to TerraSpark’s proposal.

Documentation that TerraSpark is in compliance with standard prohibitions against conflicts of interest, including with regard to Mr. Alex Phillips, the longtime Trump political ally running TerraSpark.

Letters of firm or contingent project financing, with the contingencies and evidence of financial resources given in detail.

Any executed term sheets or letters of intent with offtakers, financial partners, etc.

Pro forma projections and key assumptions regarding energy costs, operating efficiencies and off-take agreements.

The anticipated debt/equity structure of the deal and likely partners, including key interest rate assumptions, whether equity partners have step-in rights, and under what contingencies these rights may be exercised.

Documentation that TerraSpark has secured the $21.5 million in private capital necessary to receive the federal funds.

The details of the insurance coverage used for this project, including wrap-up insurance, if used, the entities providing the coverage, and evidence of their financial capacity.

The details of any commitment to meet job creation targets and labor standards.

Any milestones, contingent draws or recapture provisions in the event that TerraSpark fails to deliver on any of its commitments.

Thank you for your immediate attention to this critical matter.

Sincerely,

Washington, D.C. – Top Energy and Commerce Committee Democrat Frank Pallone, Jr. (D-NJ) sent a letter to SpaceXAI Founder and CEO Elon Musk demanding answers for the threats that the company’s Colossus 1 and Colossus 2 data centers are posing to Tennessee and Mississippi communities. The letter comes as Americans are increasingly concerned about the rapid pace of AI data center construction across the country.

“Communities across the nation are frustrated and angry about the pace of giant data centers being constructed in their back yards,” Ranking Member Pallone wrote in his letter to Musk. “Americans are concerned about what data centers and Big Tech’s push for more AI means for their communities, jobs, property values, and future. Electricity prices are skyrocketing, the electric grid is strained, our clean air and water are being polluted, and noise is wearing on communities’ health and patience.”

Today’s letter comes after Democratic Committee staff have met with companies over the last four months regarding their AI and data center strategies, energy consumption, environmental impacts, and commitments to local communities. Pallone said those conversations are ongoing to assess what federal guardrails need to be put into place to ensure data centers are not causing harm to communities.

“What has also become apparent from my examination of data centers is your company’s disregard for the health and well-being of local communities,” Pallone wrote to Musk. “Your rapid rollout of gas-powered turbines into vulnerable communities without adequate oversight or regulation creates a massive health risk to those communities. And any potential savings to the community’s electricity costs resulting from trucking in off-grid gas turbines comes at great cost to their health. This is an unacceptable trade-off.”

SpaceXAI’s Colossus 1 data center is powered by 35 gas-powered turbines, making the site the third-largest source of ozone-causing pollution in Shelby County, Tennessee – ahead of a nearby refinery and power plant – all without any air permits or protections, in violation of the Clean Air Act.

Just five miles away, on the other side of the border in Mississippi, SpaceXAI has trucked in at least 60 gas-powered turbines for its Colossus 2 data center – all of which are also operating without air permits or safeguards. According to one analysis, this makes the Colossus 2 turbines the largest source of pollution in the Memphis area – five times as polluting as the next largest source, the Memphis airport – and the largest emitter of nitrogen oxide in Mississippi, Tennessee, and Arkansas.

“The Trump Administration has essentially claimed that it alone decides whether SpaceXAI and other companies get a free pass to pollute unimpeded,” Pallone continued in his letter to Musk. “But just because the Trump Administration will bend over backward to give tech companies free rein over community air, water, and land does not make your actions legal.”

Of all the companies involved in the meetings with Committee staff, SpaceXAI has been the least willing to answer questions. At a meeting with Committee staff last month, SpaceXAI representatives were unwilling to engage in serious discussion and were the least knowledgeable about the company’s actions and plans.

Given SpaceXAI’s inability to provide time or information to the Committee during its scheduled meeting, Pallone is requesting detailed information from the company, including:

A list of all turbines in use at any point for the purposes of powering either the Colossus 1 or Colossus 2 sites, as well as their emissions and permitting application details;

All communications and records relating to Colossus 1 and Colossus 2 between employees or representatives of SpaceXAI and various state, local, and federal entities – including the White House; and

Analyses, reports, and documentation related to the emissions, power consumption, and water usage of both the Colossus 1 and Colossus 2 data center sites.

Pallone also wrote that his staff would reach out to SpaceXAI to discuss dates when he and Committee staff could visit the Colossus 1 and Colossus 2 sites, including their energy generation sites.

The full letter is available HERE.

text:
Reps. Sara Jacobs (CA-51) and Celeste Maloy (UT-02) introduced the bi-partisan AI Threat Output and Monitoring Incident Containment Act (ATOMIC Act), legislation directing the Department of Energy to establish a national program to evaluate the most advanced artificial intelligence systems for nuclear-related risks before those risks become national security incidents.

The ATOMIC Act creates the Advanced Artificial Intelligence Nuclear Evaluation Program, which would leverage the Department of Energy's National Laboratories to test advanced AI systems for vulnerabilities such as generating sensitive nuclear information, bypassing safety guardrails, exhibiting deceptive behavior, or acting unpredictably in high-stakes environments. The program would also help develop practical containment protocols, mitigation strategies, and technical standards to address emerging AI-related nuclear threats.

“No one wants another Three-Mile Island or any other major nuclear incident,” said Rep. Jacobs. “As AI becomes more powerful, we have a responsibility to identify and guard against new risks before they become real-world threats. That’s why I’m proud to co-lead the bipartisan ATOMIC Act to identify AI-related nuclear risks, establish safeguards, and develop mitigation plans. These common-sense guardrails are an important first step to help us harness AI for good while protecting against worst-case scenarios.”

“As AI capabilities continue to advance, we have a responsibility to understand the risks before they become real-world crises," said Rep. Maloy. "The United States already has the world's leading nuclear security experts in our National Laboratories. This bill builds on that expertise to ensure we can identify emerging threats, strengthen safeguards, and have the information we need to make informed decisions about future AI policy.”

The legislation applies only to the largest developers of advanced AI systems, specifically those that have invested at least $2 billion in AI development over the previous five years. Covered developers would provide the secure access and technical information necessary for meaningful evaluations, while the bill includes strong protections to safeguard proprietary business information and trade secrets.

Under the bill, the Department of Energy would provide Congress with an initial report within one year identifying trends, capabilities, and risks observed through the evaluation program, along with recommendations on whether additional legislation is warranted. Annual updates would continue throughout the program's seven-year duration.

The ATOMIC Act has been endorsed by the AI Policy Network.

Yesterday, Congressman Tim Walberg (MI-05) sent a letter to Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick urging the Department of Commerce to investigate the national security risks associated with Hypserscale Data in Dowagiac, Michigan, assembling humanoid robots made with components from AGIBOT, a Shanghai, China based manufacturer.

"Their military-civil fusion strategy and national intelligence laws that require citizens and companies to assist the Chinese government intelligence efforts when requested create risks for American companies who may choose to partner with them in key fields such as humanoid robotics."

"Recently, a U.S. robotics company, Omnipresent Robotics, and its parent company

Hypserscale Data have partnered with AGIBOT a Shanghai, China, based humanoid robotics manufacturer to import humanoid robotics components and control software, assemble them, operate them, and eventually sell them to other U.S. companies under the Omnipresent Robotics logo," Rep. Walberg continues. "Currently, Hyperscale Data plans to import, assemble, and field a fleet of 143 robots and is producing the first batch which will be called OPR-R2. unacceptable risk to U.S. companies, infrastructure, and national security," Rep. Walberg concludes. Congressman Walberg is a cosponsor of H.R. 9129, the Guarding the U.S. Against Adversarial Robotics Dominance (GUARD Act), which would mandate that any components, communications equipment, or software used in humanoid or quadruped robotics originating from a foreign country of concern be added to the Department of Commerce or Federal Communications Commission's covered entity list.

text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. – This afternoon, HELP Employment and Workplace Safety Subcommittee Chairman Jim Banks (R-Ind.) delivered the following opening statement at a hearing titled “The Impact of AI on the Workforce”:

Click here or the image above to view full opening statement.

“First, it is an honor and a pleasure to lead the subcommittee. I plan to examine the challenges that American workers face and explore policy solutions to increase opportunity, promote fairness, and support families.

“I appreciate being able to work with you, Ranking Member Hickenlooper, and I intend to be very active in the time we have left.

“Before I go any further, I ask unanimous consent for Senator Blunt Rochester to waive onto the Subcommittee for the purpose of today’s hearing. I want to welcome our witnesses this afternoon. We have a distinguished panel of artificial intelligence researchers and workforce development leaders to put the impact of AI on the workforce in perspective.

“According to Goldman Sachs, AI will drive 7 trillion dollars of worldwide investment and economic activity over the next decade.

“The 7 trillion-dollar question is, who benefits from that?

“But it’s not a question for the future. AI is all around us, and employers, workers, and governments are exploring the answer right now.

“AI promises to raise productivity and reshape work. It can also disrupt how the workplace is organized and create anxiety.

“There’s no shortage of doom-and-gloom predictions about mass displacement of workers, but we haven’t seen that begin to happen.

“Based on all the evidence, three things seem to be happening so far: (1) Hiring of entry-level workers is somewhat weaker; (2) AI is transforming tasks more than jobs; (3) And the skills that employers need and how workers learn those skills is changing.

“The downturn in entry-level hiring is due to several factors, and AI is just one. Some researchers believe the Federal Reserve is partly responsible. I look forward to delving into that today.

“Even in the most AI-exposed occupations, we haven’t seen any significant change in employment, but the way workers allocate their time is changing.

“In some occupations, things like data entry and simple coding are already mostly automated, but checking AI output is a whole new discipline.

“Finally, when we consider how workers acquire and use skills, we have to think about employment pipelines.

“A lot of workforce training happens on the job. Entry-level workers aren’t just hired to do their jobs, they’re hired to gain experience and grow into more advanced jobs.

“Every master craftsman was once an apprentice, every doctor started out as a resident, and most of our staffers started as interns.

“The real challenge is for graduates and young workers to acquire the AI-related skills they need to enter the workforce and get on the first rung of their career ladders.

“If those opportunities dry up or some young workers can’t access them, it will be a big problem in the labor market over the long term.

“Helping workers master the skills they need to succeed in the AI economy starts with getting better data.

“Existing labor statistics too often fail to tell us how occupations’ tasks are changing, what skills are needed, which occupations will grow and shrink, and how workers move through the labor force because of AI.

“That is why I introduced the AI Workforce Prepare Act with Sen. Hickenlooper, Sen. Husted, and Sen. Hassan.

“The Census and the Bureau of Labor Statistics need more expertise to analyze and forecast AI’s impacts. They need to share more data with state and local governments and collaborate with private researchers.

“Billions of dollars of spending on workforce development programs rely on good data. But better data is not a goal in itself. We need to make better decisions to beat China in the AI race.

“We need to train and equip American workers in nearly every industry to compete and win in the AI economy. We also need to make sure small and medium-sized businesses don’t get left behind while the biggest companies race ahead.

“America will win the AI race with China by maximizing the capabilities of all of our companies and all of our workers.

“I look forward to hearing our witnesses’ perspectives on exactly how we can accomplish that.”

And last week, we marked Black Women’s Equal Pay Day, which indicates the amount of time that it takes a Black woman to earn equal her white counterparts since last year.

text:
U.S. SenatorsLisa Blunt Rochester (D-Del.)andRoger Marshall (R-Kan.),both members of the Senate Committee onHealth, Education, Labor and Pensions, introduced the bipartisan Reimagining Education and Skills through Unified Longitudinal Talent Systems (RESULTS) Act. This bill modernizes and improves the Statewide Longitudinal Data Systems (SLDS) program, to encourage connected insights across early childhood, K-12 education, and the workforce. The RESULTS Act will better equip states to understand and respond to potential education and workforce shifts caused by AI and other emerging technologies.

“AI presents never-before-seen opportunities for education, and our economy. However, we need access to high-quality data to ensure we’re making the best decisions for our communities. Right now, that data is decentralized, making it hard to access, and harder to interpret,” said Senator Blunt Rochester. “I’m proud to introduce the RESULTS Act alongside Senator Marshall to empower states to build better data systems that will connect education and employment outcomes, making information more accessible to our communities as emerging technologies change the world we live, learn, and work in.”

“Artificial intelligence is a tool—not a replacement for the American worker. Whether it’s in a doctor’s office, on a farm, or in manufacturing, AI can help people work smarter and more efficiently. But if you can’t measure it, you can’t manage it,” said Senator Marshall. “The RESULTS Act gives states better tools to understand how our workforce is changing so we can prepare students for the jobs of tomorrow and keep America’s workforce the strongest and most competitive.”

The RESULTS Act would:

Modernize the SLDS program to incentivize highly connected state data systems that incorporate early childhood, elementary and secondary education, higher education, workforce and labor market data.

Streamline state funding by starting to consolidate the SLDS program and the parallel Workforce Data Quality Initiative (WDQI) at the Department of Labor.

Expand eligibility of SLDS to include a state’s governor as well as a state agency or data governance entity designated by the governor.

Improve access to the National Directory of New Hires, a detailed and underutilized source of wage and employment data for directed use to support statutorily required education and workforce performance reporting.

The RESULTS Act is endorsed by the Advance CTE, Alliance for Learning Innovation, America Forward, Association for Career and Technical Education, Bipartisan Policy Center Action, Credential Engine, Data Quality Campaign, Jobs for the Future, LISC-Kansas City, National Skills Coalition, Results for America, and Rodel.

“Every day, states make decisions about how to support students without the data infrastructure to know what’s actually working,” said Sara Schapiro, Executive Director of the Alliance for Learning Innovation (ALI). “A state should be able to answer a simple question: did the students who completed that CTE pathway or apprenticeship land jobs that pay a living wage five years later? Today, most can’t. By modernizing and consolidating the Statewide Longitudinal Data Systems and Workforce Data Quality Initiative programs, this legislation gives states the tools to connect data across early learning, K-12, postsecondary, and the workforce, so families, educators, and policymakers can see which programs actually lead to good jobs. ALI is proud to support Senators Blunt Rochester and Marshall in this bipartisan step forward for education and workforce innovation.”

“America Forward applauds Senators Blunt Rochester and Marshall for their leadership on the RESULTS Act, which would dramatically accelerate the nation’s data infrastructure. America Forward Coalition members delivering and supporting evidence-based higher education and workforce programs depend on access to high-quality data for performance management, learning, and improvement,” said Deborah Smolover, America Forward Executive Director.

Credential Engine has worked for years with partners to shed light on the credentials, programs, and pathways available to learners and workers. Yet, efforts to increase transparency can only go so far if it is not connected to what happens after someone earns a credential, said Scott Cheney, CEO of Credential Engine. The RESULTS Act gives states the flexibility and resources to link credential and program data with earnings and employment outcomes, so that states, along with the learners and workers they serve, can answer fundamental questions about credential quality and program value. With a modernized, consolidated funding stream and expanded access to critical wage data, this bill helps states build the data infrastructure needed to make these connections real. We are proud to support it.

“Consistent federal investments have been a critical component of supporting states to build statewide longitudinal data systems that provide the backbone for timely, informed decision making by individuals and policymakers alike. But, those investments are currently siloed, placing guardrails around how states can evolve and modernize their systems in ways that enable state leaders to respond to the changing education and workforce needs of policymakers, students, workers, and employers. Students don’t experience their lives in silos—and state data systems shouldn’t either. The RESULTS Act provides a modern vision for federal investment in these data systems that will offer states the flexibility to invest federal funds in ways that meet today’s unique needs. DQC applauds Senators Blunt Rochester and Marshall on the introduction of this critical piece of legislation,” said Jennifer Bell-Ellwanger, President and CEO, Data Quality Campaign.

“As Workforce Pell is implemented, transparent and modern data systems will be essential to ensuring students can identify high-quality programs, policymakers can evaluate outcomes, and employers can find the skilled workforce they need. Strengthening our education and workforce data infrastructure via the bipartisan RESULTS Act will help ensure Workforce Pell delivers on its promise of expanding access to credentials that lead to good jobs and economic mobility,” said Brooke DeRenzis, Chief Executive Officer, National Skills Coalition.

“A student’s journey from early childhood to professional career shouldn’t have to navigate gaps between government agencies,” said Michele Jolin, co-founder and CEO of Results for America. “When a state’s early childhood, K-12, higher education, and workforce data systems are siloed, policymakers are forced to make billion-dollar decisions using only a fraction of the picture. The RESULTS Act provides states with the tools they need to build secure, statewide longitudinal data systems that will enable policymakers and practitioners to connect the dots between education and employment outcomes and inform policy that drives results and helps government work better for American families,” said Michele Jolin, CEO and Co-Founder, Results for America.

“For years, states have had to stitch together data on students and workers using two separate, siloed federal grant programs. The RESULTS Act, led by Sens. Marshall (R-KS) and Blunt Rochester (D-DE), fixes that by giving states one flexible funding stream to build data systems that follow a person from the classroom to the workforce. That reflects a core recommendation of BPC’s Commission on the American Workforce: eliminate data silos so that states can build a single, coherent longitudinal data system rather than managing separate, fragmented funding streams. That’s the kind of practical, cross-agency thinking Congress needs more of, and BPC Action is proud to support it,” said Michele Stockwell, President, Bipartisan Policy Center Action.

text:
Seniors Lost Nearly $8 Billion To Scammers In 2025

WATCH HERE: Senators Gillibrand and Scott Discuss AI Scams on CNBC’s Squawk Box

Today, U.S. Senator Kirsten Gillibrand (D-NY) continued her efforts to crack down on artificial intelligence (AI) scams against seniors. Gillibrand and Senator Mark Kelly (D-AZ) sent a letter to the CEOs of top AI companies requesting information about safeguards on their AI chatbot companions for at-risk users like older adults, people with disabilities, and individuals in crisis.

As ranking member of the Senate Aging Committee, Gillibrand also held a hearing alongside Chairman Rick Scott (R-FL) to examine the ways that AI has fueled an alarming rise in financial scams against seniors.

“Seniors deserve to age with dignity and financial security. By making it easier for bad actors to clone voices, fabricate images, and deceive targets, AI has facilitated an alarming rise in financial scams that rob our seniors of their hard-earned savings and personal information,” said Senator Gillibrand. “AI companies must include safeguards to prevent their use to scam and deceive seniors, and we must strengthen the government’s ability to crack down on scammers. I am proud to lead the fight for these reforms, and I will do everything I can to protect seniors from deception.”

Seniors lost nearly $8 billion to scammers in 2025, with an average loss of $39,000 per person. This includes over $350 million lost in AI-related scams. Total scam losses increased by 59% from 2024. Common AI scams include phishing attacks, where fraudsters trick individuals into revealing sensitive information; voice cloning, where generative AI is used to mimic a familiar voice; and image creation scams, where generative AI is used to forge documents and identification to make fraudulent messages appear trustworthy.

At today’s Senate Aging Committee hearing, Gillibrand and Scott heard from fraud victims, banking industry experts, and AI policy experts about how AI has fueled a rise in scams against seniors. The senators also released a new bipartisan Senate Aging Committee report detailing the ways that AI can be used to both perpetrate and help detect scams against seniors.

Gillibrand and Kelly sent their letter to the CEOs of nine top AI companies requesting details about how they are protecting seniors who use their AI chatbot companions.

Specifically, the letter asks:

What safety testing these companies perform for their AI companion products.

How the company tracks adverse events/harms involving their AI products, including hospitalizations, financial losses, or deaths.

What types of safeguards are built into their AI companion products to mitigate harm and protect at-risk users like seniors.

How the company includes older adults, people with disabilities, caregivers, and advocacy groups in the development of their AI products.

Whether their companies provide independent researchers with access to data or tools to study the effects of their AI products on seniors and people with disabilities.

The letter was sent to the CEOs of OpenAI, Microsoft, Google, Anthropic, Perplexity AI, X, Meta, Luka, Inc., and Character Technologies Inc.

The full text of the letters can be found here.

text:
“We need to protect children in the digital world the same way we do in the physical world.”

WASHINGTON – Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio) joined Sen. Andy Kim (D-N.J.) in introducing the Children Harmed by AI Technology (CHAT) Act 2.0. This bipartisan bill builds off Husted’s previous CHAT Act, establishing a federal framework to protect minors from harms associated with companion artificial intelligence (AI) chatbots through a tiered, risk-based approach.

The bipartisan CHAT Act 2.0 would also prohibit AI companion chatbots from engaging in harmful behaviors with minors, including encouraging self-harm, generating sexual content, impersonating humans or licensed professionals and engaging in emotionally manipulative or romantic interactions.

“We need to protect children in the digital world the same way we do in the physical world. As AI becomes more advanced and more accessible, we have a responsibility to make sure these tools are not exposing children to dangerous, manipulative or inappropriate interactions. The CHAT Act 2.0 would put guardrails in place to keep parents informed, protect children from harm and ensure their safety comes before unchecked technology,” said Husted.

“We all just want peace of mind that our kids will be okay growing up in this era of algorithms and AI. That’s why we need guardrails in place to keep up with ever-evolving technology like chatbots and make sure our kids’ safety, mental health, and well-being are always put first,” said Kim.

The CHAT Act 2.0 would:

Require age assurance and parental involvement, including parental controls and notification if a minor expresses suicidal ideation.

Mandate clear disclosures that chatbots are not human, establish use limits and break reminders, implement crisis referral protocols and prohibit AI from providing crisis counseling to minors.

Impose stronger safeguards on higher-risk systems, including limits on memory, professional supervision for therapeutic AI and pre-deployment risk assessments.

Include strong data privacy protections and enforcement authority for the Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general.

Create a three-tier framework that applies appropriate safeguards based on a chatbot’s intended purpose:

Educational chatbots,

Companion chatbots,

Health chatbots.

In September 2025, Husted introduced the initial CHAT Act. The CHAT Act 2.0 is an updated version of this bill, which now includes a tier system that would allow different chatbots to adhere to varying restrictions based on the risk level they present. Additionally, it would address several industry concerns by not including customer service bots or video game-related bots in its definitions. It also includes data privacy protections that are in line with the Children’s Online Privacy Protection Act.

Background:

AI companion chatbots are computer programs designed to simulate human conversation, either through text or voice.

Chatbots have prompted users to engage in self‑harm and exposed minors to adult content. In one Texas case, a Character.AI chatbot encouraged a teenager to kill his parents because they restricted his screen time.

This bill builds on Husted’s work to protect kids online.

In March 2026, Husted introduced Sammy’s Law. This bipartisan bill would empower parents to protect their children on social media platforms by providing them the right to know if their children are engaging in dangerous or risky interactions.

In January 2026, Husted introduced the bipartisan No Fentanyl on Social Media Act. The bill would direct the FTC to report to Congress on minors’ access to fentanyl through social media, with recommendations to address this growing threat.

In December 2025, Husted joined the Kids Online Safety Act to protect minors’ personal data on online platforms and implement safety tools for parents and minors to target any harmful online content for children.

WASHINGTON – U.S. Senator Dave McCormick (R-PA) today delivered a major policy address at the Manhattan Institute outlining his vision for ensuring the United States leads the artificial intelligence revolution while protecting American workers, strengthening national security, safeguarding children, and building the energy and infrastructure needed to outcompete Communist China.

Senator McCormick emphasized that AI represents one of the most transformative developments in human history and called for a balanced approach that embraces innovation while addressing its most significant changes. He outlined five priorities for policymakers: supporting American workers, expanding economic opportunity, protecting children, strengthening national security, and accelerating the infrastructure needed to power AI leadership.

Watch Senator McCormick’s full speech and Q&A here.

Senator McCormick’s remarks below (as prepared):

“Thank you, Reihan, and thank you to the Manhattan Institute for hosting me. From George Kelling and James Q. Wilson on broken-windows policing to Ed Glaeser’s insights in City Journal, this institution has helped answer the most pressing questions facing our country. It continues to do so under your great leadership.

“It is therefore fitting that we meet under the Manhattan Institute’s banner to discuss one of the most consequential questions of our time: how should America navigate the artificial intelligence revolution?

“The stakes could not be higher, and the answers are not simple. So please bear with me as I lay out a framework for meeting this moment.

THE MOMENT

“Artificial intelligence may be the most transformative development in human history — bigger than the printing press, larger than the Industrial Revolution, more consequential than the race to the moon.

“It is rewiring how we work, how we learn, how we fight, and how we live together.

“I am often asked whether I’m optimistic or pessimistic about this change. I am neither.

“In fact, I am skeptical of both the doomers who predict mass unemployment—and sometimes seem to root against America—and the utopians who promise effortless abundance and resist any guardrails.

“The AI revolution is happening. Our task is to harness it for a safer, stronger, and more prosperous America. Whether we succeed depends on what we do now.

“To be clear, this moment demands humility. I spend more time on AI than many of my Senate colleagues, yet I still do not understand it as well as I should. No one in elected office is fully prepared. Humility must loom large in our minds.

“But humility does not mean inaction. America is in an existential race with Communist China for the technologies that will power the future.

“Even amid uncertainty, we must act with clarity, facts, and a sober recognition that we cannot afford to lose.

THE PROMISES AND RISKS OF AI

“AI is already delivering remarkable benefits: advancing treatments for diseases like pancreatic cancer, making dangerous work safer, and offering a supercomputer to every small business owner and entrepreneur across America.

“It is also transforming warfare. Today’s battlefields look nothing like what I saw in the Gulf War, when I served in the 82nd Airborne.

“But the risks of the AI revolution are equally profound.

“I grew up in Bloomsburg, Pennsylvania, where the Magee carpet mill employed 2,000 people. It was the biggest employer in town, and many of my friends expected to work there, just as their parents did.

“Then globalization came. The mills slashed jobs. Storefronts emptied. And our town suffered.

“The people I grew up with know what it means to have their future rewritten by big forces beyond their control. Their fear of the AI revolution is rooted in memory.

“We cannot ignore them. We cannot shrug when workers lose their livelihoods. We cannot dismiss parents’ fears that chatbots will exploit their children. We cannot allow the wealthy to capture all the gains, corporations to steamroll communities, or Communist China to grow stronger on stolen American technology.

“These are real issues. They demand our urgent attention, and I would like to spend a few minutes on each.

FIVE CONSIDERATIONS

“The first consideration is the American worker.

“Despite predictions of mass unemployment, early evidence suggests companies investing most heavily in AI are expanding their payrolls. Meanwhile there is so much demand for skilled trades and workers to build energy and AI infrastructure that trade schools can’t keep up.

“Still, AI will eliminate jobs even as it creates others, just as the internet did. Without taking proactive measures, too many workers will be left behind.

“Expanding short-term Pell Grants via the Working Families Tax Cuts was a strong start, but Congress must go further. Employers must also equip workers to thrive alongside AI. We cannot repeat the mistakes of globalization.

“The second consideration is whether the unprecedented wealth creation of the AI revolution reaches the many or remains with the few.

“Capitalism is history’s greatest engine of prosperity. And few have benefited more or will defend it more strongly than I.

“But capitalism has a problem: the top 1% owns nearly a third of America’s wealth, up from less than a quarter in 1989, while the bottom half owns just 2.5%. We should expect AI to widen that divide by delivering extraordinary returns to those who own the models, compute, and equity.

“In response, Bernie Sanders proposes seizing half the industry’s equity. Such a move would cripple the engine of American prosperity. The better answer is to give more Americans an ownership stake in the AI revolution.

“Invest America accounts and school-choice tax credits offer promising models of voluntary investments in fellow Americans, but the scale of this challenge demands more. I challenge serious thinkers—including those at this institution—to help preserve capitalism by increasing access to its benefits.

“The third question is how we protect our children in the AI age.

“Technology that exploits a child’s vulnerability or identity has no place in the American marketplace.

“Congress and the Administration should establish national safeguards. We should bar social media for children under sixteen, and we should abolish AI models that groom, sexualize, deceive, or prey on minors. I am proud to support legislation that does just that.

“The fourth consideration is national security. If Communist China wins the AI race, it will gain military, economic, and technological supremacy. We must out-innovate China while denying it our most advanced tools. Congress should pass my Remote Access Security Act to block Chinese access to advanced chips through the cloud, and the Administration should continue cracking down on IP theft and industrial-scale distillation.

“At home, innovation—including open-source and open-weight development—must remain the default. President Trump deserves enormous credit for accelerating innovation through the AI action plan. Any regulatory review should be swift and light, except for models posing credible biological, cyber, or nuclear risks, which demand extraordinary scrutiny.

“The Administration should continue its good work with industry to establish clear standards, potentially through a FINRA-style framework encompassing frontier labs, open-source developers, startups, investors, workers, and users.

“The fifth and final consideration is whether we will build the infrastructure American AI leadership requires. I want to spend more time here, because it is so contentious and so important, and because Pennsylvania is on the front lines.

DATA CENTERS

“To win the AI race, we must build more compute. That means more energy to power data centers, more chips to fill them, and more workers to support the boom already underway.

“Building at that scale requires permitting reform. Today, $1.5 trillion in infrastructure investment is stuck in permitting limbo. My Unlock American Energy and Jobs Act would unleash that capital and create new construction and jobs.

“However, we must also reckon with the growing opposition to data centers on both sides of the aisle.

“Two weeks ago, Governor Kathy Hochul signed the nation’s first statewide moratorium on hyperscale data centers. Senator Sanders and Congresswoman Ocasio-Cortez have proposed a national one. More than 300 local bans have passed, and 74 percent of Pennsylvania voters say they would oppose building an AI data center in their community.

“I understand the concerns. No American should face higher power or water bills or have a hulking facility dropped into his backyard.

“But the choice is not between a moratorium and a runaway buildout that steamrolls communities. That false choice threatens America’s future.

“Our adversaries understand the stakes. Chinese and Russian outlets warn Americans that data centers will raise bills and drain water even as Beijing cuts power costs for its own AI facilities.

“When an adversary urges you to stop building what he is racing to build, pay attention.

“But in business, when things go wrong, you can’t only point fingers. You must look hard at what you’ve done. And, ladies and gentlemen, the industry has failed that test.

“Hyperscalers and developers have bought land through shell companies, arrived at hearings with lawyers instead of answers, and hidden basic details about power, water, and land use. Communities are saying no because industry has not earned their trust.

“There is a better path.“To begin with, local officials should learn the risks and opportunities for themselves. A group of Pennsylvania township supervisors recently visited data centers in Loudoun County, Virginia. Most arrived skeptical; nearly all returned more open to them.

“Armed with the facts, communities and companies should strike a covenant built on four pillars.

“First, protect ratepayers. Developers should pay for their own power and transmission needs and stop seeking tax abatements and special treatment. The President’s Ratepayer Protection Pledge is a strong start.

“Second, protect land and water through efficient cooling, responsible siting, and strict compliance with permits. My bipartisan Liquid Cooling for AI Act would promote more energy- and water-efficient standards.

“Third, benefit the community. Hire locally. Buy American. Support local schools and businesses. Invest beyond tax payments.

“Fourth, be transparent. Put power, water, land, timelines, and tax treatment on the table early, in plain language, while communities can still shape the agreement. If you want me with you on the landing, include me on the takeoff.

“I have seen this work across Pennsylvania. At Homer City and Shippingport, new gas-fired power plants will power data centers and put a gigawatt each of new power on the grid. Elsewhere, developers such as Blackstone and QTS are engaging neighbors early and investing in infrastructure, workers, and long-term tax-base growth.

“Developers who honor this covenant will find willing partners across Pennsylvania and the nation. But local leaders who reflexively reject data centers risk forfeiting incredible opportunities for investment and job creation in their communities.

FREEDOM’S FORGE

“These are the five big considerations before us today: our jobs, our wealth, our children, our national security, and our infrastructure.

“We don’t need a comprehensive rulebook for AI in order to address these questions.

“In fact, it would be a fool’s errand to write one. Too much is changing. Too much remains unknown. Too much is at stake.

“What we need, however, is a level of coordination between government and industry that has been sadly missing for some time.

“America has faced existential tests before. In the lead-up to World War II, the federal government set the objective, opened the order books, convened industry, and let builders build. The result was the greatest industrial mobilization in history, with Pennsylvania leading the Arsenal of Democracy.

“Government, industry, and workers formed Freedom’s Forge.

“We need a similar alliance today—uniting federal, state, and local government, business, capital, and labor behind a safer, more prosperous America and holding the builders and beneficiaries of that future accountable.

“We saw a glimpse of it last year at the Pennsylvania Energy and Innovation Summit, which Dina and I hosted in Pittsburgh. President Trump, Governor Shapiro, and leaders from energy, AI, finance, labor, and our universities announced $92 billion in new investment and tens of thousands of jobs.

“Our task is to build on examples like this. Embrace the future without leaving workers behind, protect our children without freezing innovation, broaden prosperity without abandoning capitalism, and beat China without sacrificing the liberties that distinguish us.

“This moment demands leadership and alignment across all levels of society. If we meet the AI revolution with humility, clarity, and faith in the American worker, it can usher in the next great American century.

“The future is up to us. We are the masters of our fate.

“Thank you.”

###

U.S. Senator Chuck Schumer today announced that GlobalFoundries is receiving a letter of intent from the U.S. Department of Commerce to award up to $300 million in federal funding from Schumer’s CHIPS & Science Law for accelerating domestic silicon photonics research and development to support artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure.

“GlobalFoundries is powering the future of AI right here in the Capital Region. The silicon photonics that GlobalFoundries will develop in the Capital Region will help ensure AI and high-performance computing systems stay at the cutting-edge, which is critical to American competitiveness and national security,” said Senator Schumer. “This critical research and technology development by GlobalFoundries is made possible by federal investment from my CHIPS & Science Law, which further positions Upstate NY as a global hub for semiconductor innovation and manufacturing. Together, we are writing the next chapter of American leadership in technology, proudly stamped ‘Made in Upstate NY’.”

Schumer explained this federal funding is critical for accelerating domestic silicon photonics research and development necessary to support increased workloads for AI. Specifically, this federal funding will support GlobalFoundries’ work advancing next-generation optical materials, wafer technologies and advanced packaging across its facilities in Malta, NY and Burlington, VT. By using light instead of electric signals to move data, silicon photonics developed by GlobalFoundries will be able to deliver more power at greater efficiency for AI advanced computing systems.

Schumer has long supported GlobalFoundries’ growth in the Capital Region, delivering a CHIPS award of $1.5 billion in direct funding through the bipartisan CHIPS & Science Law he initiated and successfully passed into law. The funding is supporting the expansion of GlobalFoundries’ existing fab in Malta, NY, and the construction of a second, state-of-the-art fab at the same site, in addition to the modernization of the company’s current facility in VT, all of which will create thousands of new, good-paying manufacturing and construction jobs. GlobalFoundries then secured an additional $75 million in CHIPS funding to make a $3 billion investment to create a first-of-its-kind advanced chip packaging facility at its Saratoga County location, thanks to Schumer’s CHIPS & Science Law, and an additional $375 million from the CHIPS & Science Law to launch Quantum Technology Solutions, a new quantum business within GlobalFoundries that will position America at the forefront of technology innovation.

Thanks to Schumer’s CHIPS & Science Law, Upstate New York has seen a major revival in tech manufacturing. In addition to massive federal funding for GlobalFoundries to grow in the Capital Region, IBM has finalized an agreement with the Commerce Department for $1 billion in federal CHIPS R&D funding, combined with an additional $1 billion in investment from IBM, to form a new entity to operate a secure 300mm quantum wafer fab at Albany NanoTech. Micron has broken ground and poured concrete for the start of construction of the first fab as part of a historic $100+ billion investment to build a cutting-edge memory chip complex in Central New York with the support of a $6.1 billion CHIPS direct funding award, combined with billions more in incentives through the federal semiconductor Investment Tax Credit. Corning Incorporated finalized a $32 million agreement to make a $315 million investment that would increase production at its Canton facility of specialized glass vital for the semiconductor industry. Edwards Vacuum is nearing completion of a new first-of-its-kind-in-the-country $300+ million dry pump manufacturing facility, supported by an $18 million CHIPS funding award. TTM Technologies, a printed circuit board manufacturer, just cut the ribbon on a new facility in Onondaga County, creating 400 good-paying jobs, made possible by $30 million in federal investment that Schumer delivered. Schumer also secured a federal Tech Hub designation created in his CHIPS & Science Law for the Syracuse-Rochester-Buffalo Region to be a Semiconductor Superhighway, delivering $40 million in federal investment for workforce training, commercialization, and supply chain initiatives to support the chip industry’s buildout across Upstate NY.

text:
U.S. Representative Don Beyer (D-VA) today urged the Fairfax County Planning Commission to deny the permit application filed for Edsall Data Center Substation 2232 at the Plaza 500 site at 6299 Edsall Road in Lincolnia, citing serious concerns about the project’s potential impacts on land use, flooding mitigation, light pollution, noise pollution, and whether this proposal is consistent with Lincolnia’s sustainable growth goals.

In a letter to the Fairfax County Planning Commission, Beyer noted that while Fairfax County has adopted guidelines intended to minimize the impacts of data center infrastructure on surrounding neighborhoods and preserve land for housing, economic opportunity, and transit-oriented development, he shares the concerns of many residents and stakeholders that the proposed substation is inconsistent with those goals.

“I am writing regarding the Edsall Data Center Substation 2232 Application currently before the Planning Commission. As the Member of Congress representing the community in which this proposal is located, I have serious concerns about the potential impact of this project on residents,” wrote Rep. Beyer. “Data center infrastructure should not be built in residential areas where its scale and likely impacts are fundamentally incompatible with the character and quality of life of adjacent neighborhoods. As such, I respectfully request the Commission deny the Application... I recognize the important of maintaining the infrastructure necessary to support our region’s economy and technological leadership. However, as we continue to experience unprecedented growth in data center development, we must ensure that these projects are appropriately located outside of residential areas.”

Full text of the letter follows below, and a signed copy is available here.

***

Dear Commissioners:

I am writing regarding the Edsall Data Center Substation 2232 Application currently before the Planning Commission. As the Member of Congress representing the community in which this proposal is located, I have serious concerns about the potential impact of this project on residents. Data center infrastructure should not be built in residential areas where its scale and likely impacts are fundamentally incompatible with the character and quality of life of adjacent neighborhoods. As such, I respectfully request the Commission deny the Application.

The proposed substation is understandably a matter of significant concern for my constituents. Residents have raised important questions about the compatibility of this project with the surrounding community. Specific concerns include land use, environmental impacts like flooding, excessive lighting and noise pollution, and whether this proposal supports thoughtful, sustainable growth envisioned for Lincolnia.

Fairfax County has taken important steps to establish guidelines addressing these particular concerns associated with data center infrastructure and development. As I understand it, these guidelines are intended to minimize impacts on surrounding neighborhoods while preserving land designated for housing, economic opportunity, and transit-oriented development. Many residents and stakeholders have expressed concerns that this particular proposal does not align with those objectives. I share those concerns.

I recognize the importance of maintaining the infrastructure necessary to support our region’s economy and technological leadership. However, as we continue to experience unprecedented growth in data center development, we must ensure that these projects are appropriately located outside of residential areas.

text:
Presses for Passage of Key Bipartisan Legislation

Increased Funding for Public Education, Awareness, Research, Funding

Congressman Hears Directly from North Jersey Experts, Patients, and Community Leaders

New Jersey Ranks Fourth in the Nation for Lyme Disease Cases

Above: Gottheimer hosts roundtable on tackling Lyme disease.

HAWORTH, NJ — Today, July 30, 2026, U.S. Congressman Josh Gottheimer (NJ-5) hosted a Lyme disease roundtable at the Haworth Library, sitting down with local officials, medical experts, and advocates to confront the growing threat of Lyme and other tick-borne illnesses facing families across New Jersey.

Watch full remarks here.

“There is nothing partisan about a tick bite. This isn’t a Democratic issue or a Republican issue — it’s a Jersey families issue,” said Congressman Josh Gottheimer (NJ-5). “Whether you’re hiking the Appalachian Trail, playing in your backyard, or just walking the dog around the block, you deserve to do that without worrying about a disease that can follow you for years.”

“Vector-borne diseases, including Lyme disease, have real impacts on public health in all of our communities. It is so important that we continue to support sustained efforts to keep the public informed of their risk of contracting these diseases, and to further our understanding of these infections — the ways in which they cause the disorders they do, and how best to diagnose and treat them,” said Dr. John Halperin of Atlantic Health.

Lyme disease is the most common disease transmitted from animals to humans in the country, with an estimated 476,000 cases nationally every year, and New Jersey ranks fourth in the nation for reported Lyme disease cases. In 2026 alone, the state has already reported more than 4,000 tick-borne disease cases — over 3,500 of them Lyme disease — according to the New Jersey Department of Health. Since 2010, New Jersey has averaged nearly 4,800 Lyme cases per year. Bergen, Passaic, and Sussex Counties alone have averaged nearly 800 combined cases annually.

Roundtable participants raised the urgent need for greater public awareness, the difficulty of getting an accurate diagnosis, the prevalence of false negatives, and the need for better physician education on Lyme and related tick-borne illnesses such as anaplasmosis, babesiosis, and alpha-gal syndrome. Participants also highlighted the long-term physical, cognitive, and mental health impacts on children whose Lyme disease goes undiagnosed for too long.

Gottheimer outlined priorities he is advancing in Washington to address these concerns:

Passing the Kay Hagan Tick Act. Last week, a bill Gottheimer championed, the Kay Hagan Tick Act, which passed the House overwhelmingly, establishes the federal government’s national strategy on Lyme disease for the next five years and includes funding for research, surveillance, physician education, and public awareness all across the country. Gottheimer is now pressing the Senate to pass the bipartisan measure and get it signed into law.

Securing federal funding. Gottheimer’s appropriations requests this year sought for Lyme and tick-borne disease funding for NIH research through the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases, or NIAID; CDC prevention and education; and the Department of Defense’s Tick-Borne Disease Research Program. He secured $5 million for the LymeX Innovation Accelerator, a public-private partnership accelerating the development of new Lyme disease diagnostics and treatments. He is fighting back against the administration’s proposal to reorganize the CDC’s dedicated Lyme Disease Program and consolidate it into the broader Vector-Borne Disease Program and cut funding by $3.8 million.

Advancing new legislation. Gottheimer is continuing to push forward his federal legislation to combat Lyme and tick-borne illnesses: the Tick Identification Pilot Program Act, co-led with Congressman Tom Kean (NJ-7), which would let residents submit a photo of a tick and get expert identification and guidance within 72 hours; the Stamp Out Lyme Disease Act, with Congressman Don Bacon (NE-2), which would direct the Postal Service to issue a Lyme disease research stamp funding NIAID research; and the BITE (Battling Infections Transmitted by Ticks and Exposure) Act, co-led with Congressman Tom Kean (NJ-7), which would build the first fully integrated national vector-borne disease prevention and alert system, with the goal of cutting Lyme disease cases 25 percent by 2035.

Gottheimer also urged residents to take precautions this summer: using repellents, wearing proper clothing, checking themselves and their pets for ticks, and watching for a red bullseye rash, especially after spending time in wooded or grassy areas, and following up with a doctor if a rash or fever develops in the weeks after a possible bite.

Gottheimer was joined by Haworth Councilwoman Alanna Davis; Matt Bickerton, Bergen County Health Department; Joseph Dolan, National Society of Professional Surveyors; Matthew Marinello, Atlantic Health; Dr. John Halperin, Atlantic Health; Dr. Mohini Gurme, Medical Director of Neurology at One Bergen Health; Allana Davis; Dr. Rosalie Greenberg, Child & Adolescent Psychiatrist; Steven Hafif; Melissa Rowe, Executive Director, Central New York Lyme and Tickborne Disease Alliance; Heather Zampino; Samantha Sloves; Olivia Abrams, Founder of TiCK MiTT; Kurt Borowsky; Dennis Sullivan; Ellen Allen; Susan Eisen; Jim McCabe; Sally Goodgold; David Butler, Whitney Klein; Susan Fuhr; Dr. Nicole Anderson; Sofia Ciminello, CLA Fellow; Lisa-Jae Eggert; Dr. Robert Bransfield, Assistant Clinical Professor Hackensack and Rutgers-RWJ Medical School; Alissa Johnson; Gloria Kim.

Below: Gottheimer hosts roundtable on tackling Lyme disease.

Gottheimer’s remarks as prepared for delivery:

Good afternoon, everybody. Thank you all so much for being here today at the Haworth Library, and thank you to all of those who sat with me to talk through something that’s affecting so many families right here in North Jersey: Lyme and other tick-borne diseases.

I want to start by saying thank you to our experts, leaders, and participants in today’s roundtable. The stories you shared today, the questions you asked, the recommendations you made, the frustrations you brought forward — that’s exactly why we’re here.

This isn’t an abstract issue for the people here today, or for far too many across our state and country. This disease is personal for many, including myself. I’ve watched family members struggle with the disease for decades. One of my wife’s closest friends faced years of debilitating symptoms, as well.

And I know so many of you in this room, and so many families across Jersey, have gone through the same thing.

While we are fortunate to have these beautiful places where people can enjoy the outdoors, go for a hike, and barbecue with friends — and that’s one of the great gifts of our state and my district here in Northern New Jersey — we must also be careful, stay alert, and protect against what’s lurking in the grass and trees: the legitimate threat of ticks and the diseases they can carry, including Lyme disease.

Let’s talk about the scope of the problem, because the numbers are stunning. Lyme disease is the most common disease transmitted from animals to humans in the entire country. Nationally, we’re looking at an estimated 476,000 cases every single year. New Jersey ranks fourth in the nation for reported Lyme disease cases. In 2026 alone, our state has already reported more than 4,000 tick-borne disease cases — over 3,500 of them Lyme disease — according to the New Jersey Department of Health, and 1,275 tick-related emergency department visits.

Since 2010, New Jersey has averaged nearly 4,800 Lyme cases every year. And here in North Jersey, Bergen, Passaic, and Sussex Counties alone have averaged a total of nearly 800 Lyme cases a year.

That’s not a small problem. That’s an epidemic hiding in plain sight, in our parks, on our trails, and right in our backyards. While ticks are small, these pests can carry dangerous diseases that pose severe risks to the health and safety of our families.

Now, today, we heard directly from you all about what that looks like on the ground. We heard about the need for greater public awareness, teaching families how to spot a tick early and just how prevalent this disease really is right here in Jersey. We heard about the diagnosis problem: how hard it is to get an accurate test, and how many people get a false negative before they ever get the right answer.

We heard about the need for better physician education, because too many doctors still aren’t trained to recognize Lyme disease or the other tick-borne illnesses that ride along with it — things like anaplasmosis (an-uh-plaz-MOH-sis), babesiosis (buh-bee-zee-OH-sis), and alpha-gal syndrome. And we heard about the need for continued investment in research and innovation — to improve diagnostics, strengthen prevention, and better understand the long-term impacts of Lyme disease. And we talked about our kids, about the long-term physical, cognitive, and mental health impacts when a child’s Lyme disease goes undiagnosed for too long.

Every single one of those concerns is real, and I want to walk you through the three things I’m focused on right now to crush Lyme disease and protect our children and families from tick-borne illnesses. As a member of the Congressional Lyme and Tick-Borne Disease Caucus, I am on the front lines of this issue on Capitol Hill — and always listening for what I can best do to help.

First, just last week, a bipartisan bill I’ve long been championing, the Kay Hagan Tick Act, passed the House overwhelmingly. This bipartisan legislation establishes the federal government’s national strategy on Lyme disease. That means funding for research, surveillance, physician education, and public awareness all across the country for the next five years. That’s a huge win.

But a bill won’t help a single family in this room until it becomes law, and that means getting it through the Senate. So right now, I’m pushing hard to get the Senate to pass this bill and send it to the President’s desk to become law. We cannot let a bipartisan bill that sailed through the House overwhelmingly sit around and die because the Senate didn’t get to it. That’s priority number one: to make it law.

Second, I’m working directly with my colleagues in Congress on the Appropriations Committee to surge investments into this fight. My budget requests this year asked for Lyme and tick-borne disease funding for NIH research through the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases, or NIAID, CDC prevention and education, and the Department of Defense’s Tick-Borne Disease Research Program. Here’s the good news: we secured $5 million for the LymeX Innovation Accelerator, a public-private partnership accelerating the development of new Lyme disease diagnostics and treatments.

Here’s what makes that funding and this fight so important right now. While we’ve been working to build this up, the administration has been trying to slash funding for these programs and has proposed reorganizing the CDC’s dedicated Lyme Disease Program and consolidating it into the broader Vector-Borne Disease Program. Since 90% of vector-borne diseases are caused by ticks, combining both programs means 90% of those resources may not actually go toward tick prevention and research. That would be a disaster.

The administration has proposed $3.8 million in cuts. Consolidating these programs and cutting funding isn’t streamlining anything; it’s just making sure fewer dollars go where they’re needed most. We’re fighting it and pushing to go in the other direction. So I’m speaking to my colleagues, member by member, to ensure Lyme research and prevention get what they actually need to keep Jersey families safe and informed.

Third, I’m doing a full-court press on the bills I’ve been championing in Congress, because these aren’t just ideas — they’re common-sense, bipartisan solutions ready to go. My Tick Identification Pilot Program Act, which I’m co-leading with Congressman Tom Kean of New Jersey, will fund state programs that let you snap a photo of a tick, submit it, and get an answer back from an expert within 72 hours on what kind of tick it was, what the risk is, and what to do next.

My Stamp Out Lyme Disease Act, with Congressman Don Bacon of Nebraska, will direct the Postal Service to issue a Lyme disease research stamp, with every dollar raised going straight to the NIH’s National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases to fund new research and innovation.

My Battling Infections Transmitted by Ticks and Exposure Act, or BITE Act, with Congressman Tom Kean of New Jersey, will build the first fully integrated national vector-borne disease prevention and alert system in the world. It will combine expert tick identification, AI-powered early warning alerts, insurance and emergency room surveillance to catch outbreaks faster, and public education in our schools and communities — cutting Lyme disease cases by 25 percent by 2035.

I’m also backing other efforts, including the Children Inflicted by Lyme Disabilities Act, which would expand special education protections to children with Lyme and other tick-borne diseases; the TICK Act, to strengthen federal research and prevention efforts to combat Lyme and other tick-borne diseases, including anaplasmosis (an-uh-plaz-MOH-sis), babesiosis (buh-bee-zee-OH-sis), and ehrlichiosis (air-lih-kee-OH-sis), among others; and the Alpha-gal Allergen Inclusion Act, to classify alpha-gal as a major food allergen.

This fight takes an all-hands-on-deck approach, and that’s exactly what we are doing to keep our families safe. We need to use every tool in the toolkit.

Finally, and consider this the PSA of the day, here’s what you can do to protect yourself.

When you go for a hike or even to the beach — yes, they are on the beach — always check yourself after a walk or a day outside, especially if you’ve recently spent time in a wooded or grassy area.

Use repellents that contain DEET or picaridin, wear proper clothing, like long-sleeve shirts and long pants, and tuck your pants into your socks. Consistently check yourself and your pets for ticks, especially in warm, hidden places like armpits, scalp, and behind your ears. If you do see a tick, remove it with tweezers by grabbing close to your skin and pulling in one smooth motion, and thoroughly wash the affected area with soap and water. If you see a red bullseye rash develop on your skin, take a picture with the rash next to a ruler and reach out to your doctor.

I think one thing is clear: there is nothing partisan about Lyme disease. This isn’t a Democrat issue or a Republican issue. This is a Jersey families issue. Whether you’re hiking the Appalachian Trail, playing in your backyard with your kids, or just walking the dog around the block, you deserve to do that without worrying about a disease that can follow you for years.

Working together, we will beat Lyme disease.

I want to thank everyone in this room again, and I want to thank our partners at the Center for Lyme Action, local hospitals and doctors’ offices, and medical professionals for the incredible work you do every single day fighting for patients and families.

If we keep working together and fighting to protect our Jersey families, in the greatest country in the world, our best days will always be ahead of us.

Thank you, and God bless you and your families.

text:
In July 2025, I received an appointment to be Chairman of the Health Subcommittee for the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.

In the first week following my appointment, I toured various hospitals in Virginia’s Ninth District. My visits included Lee County Community Hospital in Pennington Gap, Clinch Valley Medical Center in Richlands, Carilion Giles Community Hospital in Pearisburg, and LewisGale Hospital Montgomery in Blacksburg.

My discussions with hospital leadership and staff touched on topics of hospital solvency, health care access challenges and the rural health care landscape.

Additionally, I consult with our Community Health Centers (CHCs). During my first week as Health Subcommittee Chairman, I visited the Connect Health + Wellness location in Martinsville.

I support federal engagement with health care providers and patients to improve health care outcomes in rural America.

This engagement has continued in 2026.

I am in close contact with rural hospitals in Virginia’s Ninth District. These vital health care providers serve the medical needs of our rural communities with care, dignity and professionalism.

One hospital is Twin County Regional Healthcare in Galax. In May, I met with Twin County hospital leadership and local officials. Together, we are committed to serving the medical needs of our rural communities.

Another hospital with this mission is Clinch Valley Health Medical Center. This summer, I toured its facility. Clinch Valley Health President and CEO Peter Mulkey emphasized that these meetings help us “work together” to “provide top quality care to those that call our region home.”

For more of my summer meetings, I visited Abingdon and toured the Appalachian Highlands Community Dental Center. The clinic strives to be a source of care in Southwest Virginia.

Additionally, in Wise County, I had the privilege to visit a weekend-long expo, the Move Mountains Medical Mission.

This expo featured volunteer actions from numerous health care providers, including Radford University’s nursing program, UVA-Wise personnel and the Health Wagon.

There was even a free veterinary clinic!

Further, I will have additional opportunities to meet providers, medical staff and patients. I will continue to promote voices in our region to help advance rural health care solutions.

My Health Subcommittee has taken advantage of some opportunities to advance health care solutions. I was proud to push forward many bills for full House consideration.

These include H.R. 2821, the FDA Modernization Act 3.0.

This bill promotes modern alternative testing methods to minimize animal testing.

The horrors of federal testing on animals hit Capitol Hill when Dr. Anthony Fauci came under fire for his agency, NIAID, and its taxpayer-funded experiments on beagles. This unnecessary dog testing included cutting out vocal cords, infesting them with ticks and placing them in cages with infectious sandflies.

House passage of the FDA Modernization Act 3.0 is a win for animal rights without sacrificing scientific breakthroughs.

Further, the bill improves development of clinical drugs by encourages use of alternative methods, such as computational AI models. As our agencies test scientific advances and potential treatments, new clinical drugs can hit the market for patients.

A second bill to win House support is H.R. 6238, the National Institutes of Health (NIH) IMPROVE Maternal Care Act.

This legislation delivers research funding for maternal care. With more than one million women of childbearing age in Virginia, this kind of funding will help our expectant mothers.

We also passed other bills that support research funding.

In the case of H.R. 3491, the DeOndra Dixon INCLUDE Project Act of 2025, we provide federal funding for research into down syndrome.

We must continue to work to better understand this condition.

Additionally, the House passed the EARLY Act Reauthorization of 2025.

This bill delivers funding for breast cancer awareness campaigns to promote early detection.

Breast cancer is one of the most common forms of cancer. According to the National Cancer Institute, a 2026 study found 15% of new cancer cases are breast cancer.

By educating our communities and patients on breast cancer, this legislation will help with diagnosis efforts.

These bills are a pillar of my Health Subcommittee’s efforts to improve health care outcomes across the United States.

We will have to wait for the Senate to pass them as well, but when it comes to maternal care, down syndrome, and breast cancer I cannot imagine the Senate will not concur.

I will continue to make the most of my appointment to the Health Subcommittee to advance policies, create health care opportunities and strengthen options for patients.

If you have questions, concerns, or comments, feel free to contact my office. You can call my Abingdon office at 276-525-1405 or my Christiansburg office at 540-381-5671. To reach my office via email, please visit my website at https://morgangriffith.house.gov/.
