text:
By Karen Wall, Patch Staff

Published Wed., August 26, 2026 at 5:34 am ET

MANCHESTER, NJ — The Manchester Township Council took the first step to banning artificial intelligence data centers in the township on Monday night with the introduction of an ordinance to do just that.

The ordinance, No. 26-48, was introduced before another overflow crowd that carried dozens of signs and chanted its message: "No Data Centers. No Means No."

The council had been faced with an overflow crowd at the Aug. 10 council meeting, where residents turned out in force because of rumors that a developer had approached the town about building one in the midst of the Pine Barrens.

Of particular concern was an ordinance approved in August 2025 by the council that designated a property owned by the Stavola Corporation off South Hope Chapel Road for redevelopment and included a provision that specifically included data centers as an acceptable use.

(Karen Wall/Patch)

The ordinance introduced Monday night repeals the 2025 measure. It also includes a definitive statement banning data centers in any part of Manchester.

The ordinance is scheduled for a second reading, public hearing and final vote on Sept. 14, township attorney Lauren Staiger said. It will take effect 20 days after publication of the ordinance following the final vote, in early October, Staiger said.

Council President Michele Zolezi announced the repeal ordinance at the start of the public meeting session, after the council returned from executive session discussions.

Mayor Joseph Hankins was absent from the meeting due to a prior commitment in Whiting. Zolezi said he attended the executive session to reiterate his opposition to data centers, which Hankins had expressed in a statement after the Aug. 10 meeting.

"Tonight the Council took an important step toward listening to the concerns our residents have raised," Hankins said after the meeting. "Repealing this provision removes data centers from our redevelopment plan entirely, and reflects our commitment to ensuring that future development in Manchester Township aligns with the character, resources, and priorities of our community."

"I want to thank the Council for their thoughtful consideration and swift action on this issue. Their willingness to listen and respond to the community speaks to their dedication to serving the residents of Manchester Township," Hankins said. "I also want to thank the residents who have shown up to meetings, written letters, and made their voices heard throughout this process. Local government works best when it responds to the people it serves, and this ordinance is a direct result of that engagement."

Hankins and members of the township administration had met with Ocean County Commissioner Robert Arace and U.S. Rep. Chris Smith, who represents Manchester as part of New Jersey's 4th District in the House of Representatives.

"AI data centers pose critical environmental risks and impose undue stresses on local resources — including water and electricity — which place significant financial burdens on ratepayers and residents," Smith said in a statement Monday afternoon. "The reasonable concerns of local residents must no longer be steamrolled by tech companies seeking profit over Americans’ quality of life — not on my watch."

At the meeting, residents applauded the introduction of the ordinance, but some questioned whether it will prevent a developer from getting plans for one in place before the ban takes effect.

Carl Block, Manchester's business administrator, reiterated statements from the Aug. 10 meeting that no plans have been presented to the township for any data center.

He said the 2025 ordinance that addressed redevelopment of the specific site had created the only place in the township where a data center was possible under the township's zoning, and by repealing that ordinance, that option was completely removed because it was specific to the redevelopment.

The ordinance repealing it adds a section completely banning data centers, removing any possibility in the town.

Block also said that the only way a proposal could have been considered is if a developer had filed a complete application for one with the township's planning board. Getting a planning application deemed complete is a process that doesn't happen quickly in the vast majority of cases.

Block also said following the process and the rules for putting the ordinance in place is important, because rushing the process out of fear that someone will try to sneak in a project under the wire would backfire and give the courts reason to reject it.

One man warned that the ban may be put in place, but that it doesn't mean the fight will be over.

"These guys will keep coming at us," the man said, "not just New Jersey, not just Manchester Township, but the whole country."

As happened at the Aug. 10 meeting there was a diverse range of residents who came out in opposition to data centers.

That included the "Jersey Devil," a man who came in costume with a sign urging the council to ban data centers and to protect the Kirkwood-Cohansey Aquifer, a massive underground reserve of freshwater that provides drinking water to millions of New Jersey residents.

At the microphone the man identified himself only as "JD," to the dismay of Zolezi, but he thanked the council for taking the first step to ban the centers.

He then took it a step farther, urging the council to seek more parcels to protect as open space in connection with the Ocean County Natural Lands Trust program, to avoid issues in the future.

The "Jersey Devil" made an appearance at the Manchester Township Council on Monday to advocate for a ban on data centers. (Karen Wall/Patch)

text:
WASHINGTON — Today, as Chairman of the Judiciary Subcommittee on Crime and Counterterrorism, U.S. Senator Josh Hawley (R-Mo.) launched an investigation into Flock Safety’s AI-powered web of thousands of cameras across the nation. As part of the investigation, Hawley is demanding Flock Safety CEO Garrett Langley provide answers as to what safeguards the company employs to protect Americans’ data.

The investigation is the latest initiative in Hawley’s work to protect Americans from AI surveillance and privacy threats. Just two weeks ago, Senator Hawley held a hearing exposing the exploitative practices of AI surveillance pricing and consumer data harvesting.

“As Chairman of the Senate Judiciary Subcommittee on Crime and Counterterrorism, I am investigating Flock Safety’s collection, retention, and dissemination of the data generated by its artificial intelligence surveillance cameras. In a few short years, Flock has assembled an unprecedented national surveillance network. Your company boasts more than 120,000 cameras across 49 states and more than 20 billion vehicle scans every month. The overwhelming majority of the Americans captured in those records did nothing wrong. Instead of serving discrete local investigations, as contemplated by our constitutional processes and safeguards, these camera networks harness artificial intelligence to pool what they capture into a national database that customers can search,” wrote Senator Hawley.

He continued, “To be sure, I want law enforcement to have tools to catch offenders and keep the public safe. But Americans do not surrender their privacy rights when they drive to work, drop their kids off at school, or go to church. The Supreme Court has recognized that a comprehensive, retrospective record of a person’s movements is different in kind from ordinary observation in public. Congress never authorized the network your industry has built. Your company’s internal policies are, in practice, the only safeguards for hundreds of millions of Americans. People across the country are now discovering that fact and demanding answers from their elected officials.”

“In light of this abuse of driver information, the American people want to know who has access to their personal data and how. This investigation will seek those answers. To facilitate that, please produce all documents and information specified in the attached annex no later than September 8, 2026. If you have questions about the scope of these requests, please contact my office to discuss,” Senator Hawley concluded.

Read the full letter here or below.

August 26, 2026

Garrett Langley

Chief Executive Officer

Flock Safety

3284 Northside Parkway NW

Atlanta, GA 30327

Dear Mr. Langley:

As Chairman of the Senate Judiciary Subcommittee on Crime and Counterterrorism, I am investigating Flock Safety’s collection, retention, and dissemination of the data generated by its artificial intelligence surveillance cameras.

In a few short years, Flock has assembled an unprecedented national surveillance network. Your company boasts more than 120,000 cameras across 49 states and more than 20 billion vehicle scans every month. The overwhelming majority of the Americans captured in those records did nothing wrong. Instead of serving discrete local investigations, as contemplated by our constitutional processes and safeguards, these camera networks harness artificial intelligence to pool what they capture into a national database that customers can search.

Recent examples of abuse and misuse of personal data reveal the woeful lack of safeguards in these systems. In Missouri, the St. Charles County Police Department terminated its contract this month after an audit revealed that a civilian employee had run Flock searches for personal reasons, completely unrelated to their law enforcement duties. Sadly, my home state is not an outlier. In Milwaukee, prosecutors charged a police officer who allegedly searched his girlfriend’s license plate 124 times and her former boyfriend’s plate 55 times, entering “investigation” as his justification each time. Worse still, the officer was not caught by the company’s audit systems—he was caught because a private citizen looked up his own plate on a public website.

Errors and false positives add insult to injury. A Florida woman spent 13 days in jail and faced eight felony counts, including three counts of vehicular homicide, after investigators arrested an owner based on their search of Flock’s network for a vehicle description. Prosecutors dismissed the charges seven months later when law enforcement discovered the error and arrested a different person. One California police department found that a staggering 71% of its alerts were wrong, and the Los Angeles Police Department dropped its Flock contract after an audit showed officers had stopped 161 vehicles incorrectly flagged as stolen in the space of two months.

Furthermore, once cameras collect driver data, uncertainty abounds in how your company and its customers can sell or use data. Flock’s $8.3 billion valuation comes with enormous pressure to find new commercial applications. Americans demand a full accounting for how their driver data is stored or sold.

To be sure, I want law enforcement to have tools to catch offenders and keep the public safe. But Americans do not surrender their privacy rights when they drive to work, drop their kids off at school, or go to church. The Supreme Court has recognized that a comprehensive, retrospective record of a person’s movements is different in kind from ordinary observation in public. Congress never authorized the network your industry has built. Your company’s internal policies are, in practice, the only safeguards for hundreds of millions of Americans. People across the country are now discovering that fact and demanding answers from their elected officials.

In light of this abuse of driver information, the American people want to know who has access to their personal data and how. This investigation will seek those answers. To facilitate that, please produce all documents and information specified in the attached annex no later than September 8, 2026. If you have questions about the scope of these requests, please contact my office to discuss.

Sincerely,

Josh Hawley

text:
Prediction market paid influencers have posted misinformation about elections under the label “paid partnership,” including in SAVE Act posts

WASHINGTON, D.C. — Today, U.S. Senators Alex Padilla (D-Calif.), Ranking Member of the Senate Rules and Administration Committee, and Mark Warner (D-Va.), Vice Chairman of the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence, demanded answers from the country’s largest prediction market platforms and urged them to take immediate action to protect election integrity ahead of this year’s midterm elections and end relationships with paid influencers on their platforms spreading election disinformation.

In a letter to Polymarket and Kalshi, the Senators raised concerns regarding the platforms’ practice of paying online influencers who have spread false information, including claims that U.S. federal elections are subject to widespread fraud.

“We are seriously alarmed that your marketing strategy includes paying numerous social media influencers willing to espouse unreliable information on elections,” wrote the Senators. “In doing so, we are concerned that your prediction market platforms may be subsidizing — and amplifying — social media influencers who echo President Trump’s baseless attacks and sow distrust in American elections. Ahead of the 2026 midterm elections, we urge your platforms to reevaluate this practice, thoroughly vet your paid influencers election related activities, and immediately terminate any paid influencer relationships with individuals who undermine free and fair elections.”

The Senators also highlighted the platforms’ ability to allow users to wager on government actions. They emphasized the role of paid Polymarket and Kalshi influencers in those wagers through spreading false claims of election fraud and ultimately undermining election integrity in their promoted social media posts. The Senators specifically flagged paid influencer posts about the anti-voter SAVE Act.

“In July, a series of major social media influencers, including former Congressman Matt Gaetz, all posted similar ‘paid partnership’ posts linking to Polymarket and Kalshi charts showing the odds of enactment of the SAVE Act dropping to all-time lows. As Majority Leader Thune has noted, much of the pressure on the Senate to pass the SAVE Act, rooted in false claims of widespread election fraud, comes from ‘paid influencers.’ These paid posts on X, some of which have been removed for violation of X’s policies, added commentary that either undermined confidence in U.S. election integrity, advocated for the passage of this partisan, anti-voter legislation, or both,” continued the Senators.

The Senators requested additional information from Polymarket and Kalshi about their paid influencer contracts and strategy, their policies for influencers who post about elections, whether the companies consider disinformation to be fraudulent conduct, and the vetting process of paid influencers in the context of elections.

“As your platforms work to respond to these questions, we urge you to act now to reevaluate all paid influencer relationships regarding elections, thoroughly vet all existing and future paid influencer arrangements, and immediately terminate any existing relationships with those who spread election misinformation, disinformation, or undermine the integrity of U.S. elections,” the Senators concluded.

As Ranking Member of the Senate Rules Committee with oversight over federal elections and California’s former Secretary of State, Padilla has been a leader in protecting our elections. Last month, Padilla introduced the Stop Harassment and Intimidations in Elections through Legal Defenses (SHIELD) Our Elections Act, legislation that would provide states and voters the ability to enforce federal election protections and protect voters’ ballots from seizure. In June, Padilla and Senator Jeff Merkley (D-Ore.) introduced the Fraudulent Artificial Intelligence Regulations (FAIR) Elections Act to protect voters in the face of misuse of artificial intelligence to suppress voting and voter purges amid the Trump Administration’s attacks on the right to vote and election conspiracy theories.

A list of prediction market paid influencer posts is available here.

Full letter is available here and below:

Dear Mr. Coplan and Mr. Mansour:

In operating prediction markets tied to American elections, your platforms have a responsibility not to undermine the confidence in those elections as well as an obligation to protect the integrity of the trading activities on the platforms. With the 2026 midterm elections 69 days away, we are writing to urge your companies, the largest prediction markets platforms in the United States, to assume greater responsibility and take immediate appropriate action to ensure that your platforms do not undermine confidence in American elections.

Misinformation and disinformation pose serious threats to election security and the ability to hold free and fair elections. Recent surveys show that Americans’ confidence in our elections has been falling in the wake of years of baseless attacks on the integrity of our elections, including those led by President Trump and his election denier allies. As a result of these baseless attacks, nonpartisan and bipartisan election workers have endured verbal abuse and threats of physical violence for doing their jobs, causing many experienced personnel to leave the field. By creating and aggressively promoting markets on elections, your platforms now play a significant role in shaping Americans’ perceptions of their elections.

Given this context, we are seriously alarmed that your marketing strategy includes paying numerous social media influencers willing to espouse unreliable information on elections. In doing so, we are concerned that your prediction market platforms may be subsidizing—and amplifying—social media influencers who echo President Trump’s baseless attacks and sow distrust in American elections. Ahead of the 2026 midterm elections, we urge your platforms to reevaluate this practice, thoroughly vet your paid influencers election related activities, and immediately terminate any paid influencer relationships with individuals who undermine free and fair elections.

Social media influencer content sponsored by prediction markets that contains election misinformation or disinformation is not a hypothetical concern. In June, influencers under contract with both Kalshi and Polymarket spread false conspiracy theories about recent California elections. These posts appeared on X, formerly Twitter, marked as “paid partnership,” using prediction market election odds to support baseless claims of election fraud. These posts were only taken down when reported on by the news media, and after they were viewed by millions of Americans. Yet, despite posting previous “paid partnership” posts violating Polymarket and Kalshi’s terms and conditions, some of these same influencer accounts continue to post misinformation that undermine confidence in elections as paid partners.

Polymarket has committed to keep its “markets free from deceptive, manipulative, and unfair trading practices.” Similarly, Kalshi forbids users from “intentionally provid[ing] misleading, erroneous, or fraudulent information.” Polymarket and Kalshi both forbid certain persons with the ability to influence, directly or indirectly, the outcome of the underlying event, from trading on related contracts on the platform. When election related mis- and disinformation is deployed to create false narratives, to manipulate attitudes, to obfuscate facts, and to create public perceptions derived from that mis- and disinformation, it undermines confidence in the accuracy and fairness of the markets that your platforms offer for U.S. elections.

Your companies also have independent obligations under the Commodity Exchange Act to police fraud, enforce compliance with their rules, and guard against prohibited trading practices. These obligations raise additional concerns when platforms are paying individuals to promote contracts while those same individuals may be spreading false information about the events underlying those contracts.

In addition to offering prediction markets based on election outcomes, both Kalshi and Polymarket offer users the ability to bet on government actions, including the passage of legislation or actions by the executive branch. Also relevant to election misinformation on your platforms is the betting interest in whether President Trump’s partisan, anti-voter legislation known as the SAVE Act or SAVE America Act will be enacted by certain dates. In July, a series of major social media influencers, including former Congressman Matt Gaetz, all posted similar “paid partnership” posts linking to Polymarket and Kalshi charts showing the odds of enactment of the SAVE Act dropping to all-time lows. As Majority Leader Thune has noted, much of the pressure on the Senate to pass the SAVE Act, rooted in false claims of widespread election fraud, comes from “paid influencers.” These paid posts on X, some of which have been removed for violation of X’s policies, added commentary that either undermined confidence in U.S. election integrity, advocated for the passage of this partisan, anti-voter legislation, or both. A document containing saved images of many of these posts is attached.

Some paid influencer election misinformation posts were taken down after Senate committee staff or the media alerted Polymarket, Kalshi and/or X that these posts appeared to violate X’s paid partnership policy prohibiting “[g]eo-political, political, social issues or crises for commercial purposes” as a content category for paid partnerships. In contrast, posts that were not flagged for X remain online, indicating that both Kalshi or Polymarket continue to enable the dissemination of false content undermining our nation’s elections and are not taking sufficient steps to prevent this harmful content from being published by your paid social media marketers. Prediction markets appear to place responsibility on the social media companies, rather than taking proactive measures with your marketing partners, for posts that violate your own terms and conditions. Given the public track record of many of these influencers, these types of paid sponsorship posts espousing election denial claims were foreseeable – and should not be repeated.

We appreciate your platforms’ engagement with Senate staff to answer questions about your paid influencer policies and practices. However, given the issues discussed above, serious questions remain. We therefore request written answers to the following inquiries by September 4, 2026:

Describe the standard paid influencer contract for your platform, including any restrictions, range of payment amounts, and provide a sample contract.

What criteria does a paid influencer need to meet to be considered for an influencer contract with your platform? What type of vetting do paid influencers receive before your platform finalizes a paid influencer contract?

Does your platform have a policy towards paid influencer content regarding U.S. elections? If so, please provide a copy of that policy.

Does your platform have a policy towards paid influencer content containing misinformation about elections? If so, please provide a copy of that policy.

Please explain your company’s rationale for entering into paid influencer contracts with social media influencers who have public records of spreading misinformation or disinformation about U.S. elections.

KalshiEX LLC Rulebook’s Rule 5.17(h) states that “No Person shall engage in any activity that presents a risk of harm to Kalshi, its Participants, or the public.” In the same document, Rule 5.17 (i) states that “No Person shall engage in any activity that adversely affects the integrity of the Platform or its underlying systems.”

Does Kalshi consider the spreading of mis- and disinformation about events that are the subject of event contracts as creating a risk of harm to Kalshi, its Participants, or the public?

Does Kalshi consider the spreading of mis- and disinformation about events that are the subject of event contracts as an action that adversely affects the integrity of the Kalshi Platform?

Polymarket’s Rulebook Rule 7.2(b) states that “No Participant shall engage in fraudulent or deceitful conduct. Nor shall any Participant make any untrue or misleading statement or omit a material fact.”

Does Polymarket consider the spreading of mis- and disinformation about events that are the subject of event contracts as engaging in fraudulent or deceitful conduct?

Does Polymarket consider the spreading of mis- and disinformation about events that are the subject of event contracts to be the making of an untrue or misleading statement or omit a material fact? Does Polymarket believe that mis- and disinformation is capable of changing the likelihood of events to resolve in a given way, and therefore is information that would influence the result, and payout, of an event contract?

Does your platform engage in any vetting of paid influencer content regarding U.S. elections, either before or after the influencer posts content for which they are being compensated for by your platform? Please describe.

Are paid influencers allowed to place bets in the prediction markets that they are being paid to promote, such that they could “front run” their own posts by taking positions that would likely profit following a coordinated social media influencer campaign?

Please describe the policies, procedures, surveillance systems, or other controls your respective platforms have in place to identify whether paid influencer activity may constitute or contribute to fraud, manipulation, price distortion, or other conduct prohibited by the Commodity Exchange Act, CFTC regulations, or your respective platform rules.

Have either of your platforms investigated paid influencer activity for potential violations of these obligations?

As your platforms work to respond to these questions, we urge you to act now to reevaluate all paid influencer relationships regarding elections, thoroughly vet all existing and future paid influencer arrangements, and immediately terminate any existing relationships with those who spread election misinformation, disinformation, or undermine the integrity of U.S. elections.

Thank you for your continued engagement on these issues, and we urge you to take all necessary actions to prepare for the 2026 election so that prediction markets do not cause additional harms to American election security.

Sincerely,

text:
By J. Mayhew

Published August 27, 2026 at 3:38 PM EDT

Manchester Township Council brought forth an ordinance Monday night. It bans AI data centers in the municipality. The measure, Ordinance No. 26-48, came before a packed crowd who carried signs and chanted "No Data Centers. No Means No."

The ordinance repeals a measure approved in August 2025 that designated a property owned by Stavola Corporation off South Hope Chapel Road for redevelopment. That earlier legislation included a provision listing data centers as an acceptable use.

Council President Michele Zolezi announced the repeal at the start of the public meeting session. Mayor Joseph Hankins was absent due to a prior commitment in Whiting. He attended the executive session to reiterate his opposition.

"Tonight the Council took an important step toward listening to the concerns our residents have raised," Hankins said after the meeting, according to Patch. "Repealing this provision removes data centers from our redevelopment plan entirely, and reflects our commitment to ensuring that future development in Manchester Township aligns with the character, resources, and priorities of our community."

GETTY IMAGES

The ordinance will receive a second reading, public hearing, and final vote on Sept. 14, said township attorney Lauren Staiger. It takes effect 20 days after publication following the final vote in early October.

U.S. Rep. Chris Smith, who represents the area as part of New Jersey's 4th District, issued a statement Monday afternoon supporting the ban. "AI data centers pose critical environmental risks and impose undue stresses on local resources — including water and electricity — which place significant financial burdens on ratepayers and residents," Smith said.

Residents packed the meeting for the second time this month. A packed crowd attended the Aug. 10 council meeting after rumors spread that a developer had approached the town about building a facility in the Pine Barrens.

Carl Block, the township's business administrator, said no plans have been submitted. He said the 2025 ordinance had created the only place where such a facility was possible under zoning rules, and repealing it removes that option completely.

Block said a developer could have moved forward by filing a complete application with the planning board. Getting an application deemed complete is a process that doesn't happen quickly in most cases, he said.

text:
BUTLER COUNTY, IOWA – U.S. Senate Judiciary Committee Chairman Chuck Grassley’s (R-Iowa) investigation into eight major tech companies has prompted “significantly improved” and “more actionable” reports of online child exploitation, according to a letter from the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC). These improvements have allowed law enforcement to better respond to instances of child abuse.

“Following your direct outreach to these platforms regarding these issues, NCMEC is pleased to share that each of the companies have constructively engaged with NCMEC to significantly improve their reporting to the CyberTipline… more actionable CyberTipline reports are being submitted, enabling law enforcement to better investigate offenders and safeguard children from sexual exploitation,” NCMEC wrote in a letter to Grassley.

In April 2026, Grassley opened a congressional inquiry into Meta, TikTok, Amazon, Snapchat, Discord, X.AI, Grindr and Roblox regarding the companies’ alleged failure to sufficiently report online child sexual exploitation. In June 2026, Grassley released responses from each of the companies, which explained their efforts to improve reporting processes. In August 2026, NCMEC informed Grassley that each platform had taken “substantive measures” to address its reporting deficiencies as a direct result of Grassley’s oversight.

“Protecting children online is a top legislative and oversight priority for me as Senate Judiciary Committee Chairman. I’m glad to see my investigation into child safety reporting yield real results, and I appreciate these companies for responding to my oversight. I also thank them for working with NCMEC to ensure every suspected incident of online child exploitation is detected, reported and addressed,” Grassley said. “I’ll always work to hold Big Tech accountable to the American people, and I’ll continue fighting for commonsense solutions to safeguard our nation’s children.”

Read NCMEC’s latest update HERE.

Grassley’s original inquiry can be found HERE, and the tech companies’ responses can be found HERE. A summary of NCMEC’s update can be found below:

Meta

According to NCMEC, Meta submitted nearly 11 million reports involving suspected online child exploitation to NCMEC’s CyberTipline in 2025.

Following Grassley’s oversight, Meta has:

Improved its reporting process to ensure reported conduct meets the legal threshold for CyberTipline reporting.

Increased its use of report annotations to provide additional context for law enforcement responding to incidents of child exploitation.

Resolved a technical issue that resulted in around 3,900 duplicate reports in 2025.

Updated its training and escalation protocols for reports involving suicidal ideation.

TikTok

TikTok submitted over 2.1 million reports involving suspected online child exploitation to NCMEC’s CyberTipline from January 2025 to June 2025.

Following Grassley’s oversight, TikTok has:

Significantly reduced reports of non-pertinent content.

Implemented biweekly discussions with NCMEC to improve reporting quality and accuracy.

Amazon

Amazon AI Services submitted approximately 1.1 million reports involving suspected online child exploitation to NCMEC’s CyberTipline in 2025. After human review, Amazon determined 99.6% of the reports were false positives, and 4,376 were confirmed child sexual abuse material (CSAM).

Following Grassley’s oversight, Amazon has:

Implemented human review of public-web detections to confirm instances of child sexual exploitation before submitting reports.

Improved its CyberTipline reporting process to include source URLs, file names, reported files and additional contextual information.

Conducted a comprehensive review of more than one million submitted reports and retracted false positives.

Snapchat

Snapchat submitted approximately 752,000 reports involving suspected online child exploitation to NCMEC’s CyberTipline in 2025.

Following Grassley’s oversight, Snapchat has:

Implemented new report annotations to indicate minor-to-minor interactions, sextortion and sadistic online exploitation.

Expanded use of reported incident types, including “unsolicited obscene material sent to a child.”

Refined reporting to provide evidence of an offender’s knowledge of a child’s age.

Improved its reporting process to include additional chat history to provide greater context for law enforcement.

Discord

According to NCMEC, Discord submitted nearly 490,000 reports involving suspected online child exploitation to NCMEC’s CyberTipline in 2025.

Following Grassley’s oversight, Discord has:

Reduced reporting of non-pertinent content.

Improved reporting procedures to ensure relevant user account and location information is included in CyberTipline reports or made available to law enforcement.

Improved its reporting process to include port numbers.

X.AI

X.AI submitted over 135,000 reports involving suspected online child exploitation to NCMEC’s CyberTipline in 2025.

Following Grassley’s oversight, X.AI has:

Resubmitted previous CyberTipline reports with more complete user and location information.

Improved its reporting process to include key subscriber information, including name, date of birth, email address, screen name, user identifier, registration or login IP address and profile URL.

Improved its reporting process to ensure location information is included in the majority of reports.

Improved its reporting process to include image-generation prompt information, when applicable, to provide additional investigative context.

Grindr

According to NCMEC, Grindr submitted over 111,000 reports involving suspected online child exploitation to NCMEC’s CyberTipline in 2025.

Following Grassley’s oversight, Grindr has:

Significantly improved its reporting process to more frequently include user and location information as well as key subscriber information, including display name, user identifier, login IP address, port number, device ID, estimated location and profile bio when applicable.

Resubmitted approximately 7,000 reports with updated IP and location information.

Committed to resubmitting approximately 54,000 reports with additional location information.

Established regular engagement with NCMEC and committed to participate in the 2026 CyberTipline Roundtable.

Roblox

According to NCMEC, Roblox submitted over 65,000 reports involving suspected online child exploitation to NCMEC’s CyberTipline in 2025.

Following Grassley’s oversight, Roblox has:

Significantly improved its reporting process to better identify the child victim in incidents involving multiple children.

Conducted additional training for reporting personnel.

Increased its use of report annotations to provide additional context for law enforcement.

Worked with NCMEC to improve identification and reporting of sadistic online exploitation.

Boston (August 27, 2026) - Senator Edward J. I am proud that my original law, the Children's Online Privacy Protection Act, helped hold Meta accountable, but we cannot stop here. In this emerging age of artificial intelligence, Big Tech is finding more ways to exploit our children’s data and manipulate their emotions for profit, making them and an entire generation sicker. Congress must pass my Youth AI Privacy Act to protect kids using AI chatbots and pass COPPA 2.0 to update my original law. We cannot rely on courts alone to secure strong protections for our kids’ privacy and safety — Congress must act.”

In August, Senator Markey celebrated the passage of his Youth AI Privacy Act unanimously through the Senate Commerce Committee.

Senator Markey’s COPPA 2.0 passed through the Senate unanimously in March 2026. Senator Markey is the original House author of the Children’s Online Privacy Protection Act (COPPA), passed in 1998.

WASHINGTON – Today, U.S. Senator Todd Young (R-Ind.) delivered remarks at the groundbreaking ceremony for SK hynix’s more than $4 billion semiconductor advanced packaging facility in West Lafayette. The historic investment was made possible in part by theCHIPS and Science Act, landmark legislation Senator Young helped author and pass to strengthen domestic semiconductor manufacturing and bring high-tech investment and jobs back to the United States.

The investment will establish SK hynix’s first U.S. advanced packaging facility for next-generation high-bandwidth memory (HBM), a critical technology used to power artificial intelligence. SK hynix expects the project to create approximately 7,000 direct and indirect jobs through construction, operations, partner companies, and related industries.

“SK hynix’s historic investment in West Lafayette is further proof that Indiana is leading the way in rebuilding America’s semiconductor industry,” said Senator Young. “This project will create good-paying jobs, strengthen our national and economic security, and ensure the technologies of the future are developed and manufactured here in the United States. I was proud to help make this investment possible through the CHIPS and Science Act, and I look forward to seeing the impact it will have on Hoosiers and our country for decades to come.”

SK hynix also announced a research and development partnership with Purdue University focused on advanced packaging technologies. More than 150 materials, components, and equipment partners are discussing participation in the local supply chain, further strengthening Indiana’s growing semiconductor ecosystem.

Senator Young was instrumental in the passage of the CHIPS and Science Act, which was signed into law in 2022. The law provides incentives to bring semiconductor manufacturing and research to the United States, strengthen domestic supply chains, and bolster America’s economic and national security.

The U.S. Department of Commerce awarded SK hynix up to $458 million in direct funding through the CHIPS and Science Act to support the West Lafayette project along with up to $500 million in federal loans.

Q: What is the Workforce Pell Grant?

A: It’s back to school season for families, students and teachers across the state. As students return to the classroom, schedules are filling up with homework and extracurricular activities and parents are off to the races juggling jobs, car pools and meal times. Many students are starting a new chapter with post-secondary education, including four-year colleges, community colleges and vocational programs. Studies show advanced training leads to job readiness, higher earnings and more opportunities.

However, too many students are pushed into burdensome debt seeking a four-year degree that doesn’t fit job market demands. For example, skilled trades are in growing demand and largely protected from artificial intelligence (AI) because the work can’t be replaced by automation. That’s where smart policymaking can help solve problems. I co-sponsored legislation to expand access to high-quality, short-term job training programs to help close the skills gap that I hear from employers at my annual 99 county meetings. During work on last year’s tax bill, I pushed successfully to include my bill called Promoting Employment and Lifelong Learning (PELL) Act in the final package. It amends the Higher Education Act of 1965 to provide for Workforce Pell Grants that allow eligible students to use Pell Grants for short-term, accredited programs that provide workforce-focused credentials that meet employer needs.

I’m pleased Iowa is the very first recipient of the nation’s first Workforce Pell Grant program. Eligible students at Iowa Central Community College in Fort Dodge can use federal Pell Grant dollars to enroll in its Emergency Medical Technician Program. The 14-week program prepares students for public safety jobs that will fill a critical need in local communities across the state. These students will start their jobs with little to no debt and have the training credentials to launch good careers, provide for their families and serve their neighbors.

Q: What are you hearing from small businesses at your county meetings?

A: No matter the size of the community, small businesses make up the lion’s share of employers across Iowa, and support nearly half the workforce. During my annual 99 county meetings, I regularly hold Q&As at small businesses, factories and manufacturing facilities so that I can hear directly from the workers and small business owners who can’t take time off to come to an open town meeting. I want to hear about challenges they face and learn what’s on their minds. From decades-old family-owned businesses to start-up businesses opening their doors, I’m always impressed with the entrepreneurism and hard work that Iowa workers and employers put in each and every day to climb America’s ladder of prosperity and serve their communities. I’ve also come to the conclusion that Iowans don’t brag enough about their high-quality products and services, so I’m particularly glad to get a first-hand look at these businesses. Iowans set a high benchmark for a strong work ethic and it shows with workforce productivity and state-of-the-art manufacturing and technology.

text:
WASHINGTON — U.S. Senator Josh Hawley (R-Mo.) penned an op-ed in The Daily Wire following the announcement of his investigation into companies like Flock, with its network of 120,000 AI-powered cameras across the United States. Senator Hawley raises concerns about how Flock’s collection of citizens’ data and personal information poses privacy threats and potentially violates existing laws.

Read the full op-ed here or below.

Every month, AI-powered cameras take 20 billion snapshots of cars in America. In almost every case, these photos capture drivers who did nothing wrong. These are regular folks on their way to work, picking up kids at school, or driving to church. Now, they are understandably asking what happens to the data captured by a network of more than 120,000 of these Flock cameras nationwide.

Even though this is new technology, it raises an issue older than our country itself. In 1761, a Boston lawyer named James Otis went to court to fight against something called writs of assistance, which gave customs officers virtually unlimited authority to search anywhere for smuggled goods. After the colonial court did not stop the writs, John Adams said American independence was born “then and there.” Otis never argued against law enforcement or the need for searches. He objected to open-ended authority without any limiting rules.

Today, Congress has not written any rules governing the data captured by national AI camera networks built by Flock Safety and similar companies. It may be governed by older statutes, and should have Fourth Amendment limits, but those are unsettled questions. For now, for practical purposes, the only privacy protections for hundreds of millions of Americans are those found in one company’s internal policies. I don’t know if Flock has broken the law, but I do know that technology is moving faster than Congress is keeping up. So I have opened an investigation in the Senate Judiciary Subcommittee on Crime and Counterterrorism, which I chair, into how this data is collected, retained, searched, and sold.

I heard about this issue in my home state of Missouri. The St. Charles County Police Department canceled its Flock contract this month, after an audit found a civilian employee running searches for personal reasons. Sadly, my state is not alone. In Milwaukee, prosecutors charged an officer with searching his girlfriend’s plate 124 times and her former boyfriend’s plate 55 times, typing the word “investigation” in the software’s justification field each time. Worse still, the system’s audit didn’t catch him; a private citizen did, after looking up his plate on a public website.

Adding insult to injury, the systems make mistakes. A Florida woman spent 13 days in jail on eight felony counts, three for vehicular homicide, after investigators searched Flock’s network for a vehicle description and arrested the owner. The prosecutors later dropped the charges because they had the wrong person. Los Angeles dropped its Flock contract after an audit found officers had stopped 161 drivers wrongly flagged as driving stolen cars. Another California police department found that 71 percent of its alerts were wrong.

Then we consider what happens to records generated by these cameras. Flock boasts an $8.3 billion valuation, which brings commercial pressures. Americans deserve to know whether and how their driving data is licensed, sold, and used. There are also concerns about whether data is sent or stored abroad. For example, reporters have described Flock using gig workers in the Philippines to classify data captured by cameras. Powerful AI models also automate parts of the process, supercharging these concerns.

All that said, I want police to have the tools they need. Cameras can help recover stolen cars, find missing children, and catch fleeing criminals. But people are concerned when private companies build unprecedented databases of personal information and want reasonable safeguards for that data. And the Supreme Court has found that people have a reasonable expectation of privacy against a “comprehensive” record of where they’ve been. Americans do not surrender all their privacy rights every time they leave the house.

So I have posed common-sense questions to Flock about how long it keeps data, who controls it, who can search it, what protections are in place, and who, if anyone, is buying what the cameras see.

I hope the company will commit to resolving these questions. But even if it does, Congress should not just take its word at face value; we should write protections into law. These safeguards must apply to every company and endure longer than the tenure of current CEOs. More fundamentally, the rules protecting Americans should be set by law and by the people, not by venture capital funds, AI executives, or big tech companies.

From the corporate world to the average household, things are already very different than they were even a couple years ago. AI has the potential to be the greatest information innovation since the printing press. Still, technology is only as good as our ability to use it well and for the right reasons − especially when it comes to our kids and grandkids.

…

Replacing human interaction with AI is a clear threat to every child’s interpersonal development. AI is a tool. It’s not supposed to be a catch-all, stand-in for therapists, doctors, lawyers, scientists, poets, or philosophers. It can never replace human connection. It does not possess the humanity we need to support one another or to override a parent’s guidance.”

…

If we want America to lead the world in innovation for the next generation, our children need to learn how to use the tools of the future. It’s up to us to make sure they can do it safely. The Safeguard Kids Act does just that; Congress should pass it without delay.”

Today, Senator Reverend Raphael Warnock met with residents in Effingham County to discuss the impact of OpenAI’s proposed data center on their community

In July, OpenAI announced it would construct a 3.2-gigawatt data center in Effingham County, Georgia

Senator Warnock called for a moratorium on data center construction that can only be lifted for specific projects if certain safeguards around utility bills, transparency, and pollution are put in place

VIDEO: Senator Reverend Warnock Calls for Statewide Data Center Moratorium

Senator Reverend Warnock: “The lack of transparency here in Effingham County and in counties across our state and across the country is unacceptable, and that’s why today I’m calling for a moratorium on data centers”

Guyton, GA – Today, U.S. Senator Reverend Raphael Warnock (D-GA) visited the proposed site of OpenAI’s new 3.2-gigawatt data center in Effingham County. Senator Warnock viewed the site of the proposed project with Effingham resident John Smith who lives across the street from the site. Then, Senator Warnock met with several residents and members of the Protect Effingham Alliance who raised serious concerns about the impact of OpenAI’s plan on their community, specifically higher utility costs and more water, light, and noise pollution.

After speaking with local residents, Senator Warnock announced his support for a statewide moratorium on data center construction.

Under Senator Warnock’s proposal, the moratorium can be lifted for a specific project only if:

There are no water or electric bill increases because of the data center

There are no sweetheart tax giveaways to developers

There are no NDAs

The data center will not cause air and water pollution

There is no ambiguity around noise and light pollution

“Data center developers across the country are not operating in partnership with communities, and that’s why everyday citizens on both sides of the aisle are rightly and equally concerned about this,” said Senator Warnock. “The lack of transparency here in Effingham County and in counties across our state and across the country is unacceptable, and that’s why today I’m calling for a moratorium on data centers.”

Earlier this year, OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT, announced plans to construct a new 1,400-acre data center in Effingham County, Georgia. The $20 billion proposal, named “Project Camellia,” will require 3.2 gigawatts, the equivalent of providing power for 2.3 million homes.

Effingham County residents were effectively excluded from the decision-making process, despite well-founded concerns that “Project Camellia” could raise electricity rates, create disruptive light and noise pollution, and otherwise affect the local community and nearby elementary school.

Earlier this year, Senator Warnock sent a letter calling on the Environmental Protection Agency to provide local communities with tools, resources, best practices, and protections as they negotiate with multi-billion-dollar data center corporations. Specifically, this letter focused on concerns about data centers straining community water supplies, especially while Georgia experiences a historic drought.

Washington, D.C. — Today, Congressmen Tom Barrett (MI-07), Greg Landsman (OH-01), Buddy Carter (GA-01), and Kim Schrier (WA-08) introduced the bipartisan Doctors Not AI Act to ensure that artificial intelligence cannot make or dictate health insurance coverage decisions involving medical judgment. The bill would require a qualified, licensed health care professional, exercising independent clinical judgment, to make any decision that a particular procedure, treatment, or prescription is not medically necessary.

“Artificial intelligence should never replace the judgment of a doctor,” said Barrett. “When it comes to someone’s health and well-being, the outcome is too important to leave it up to an algorithm. This bill makes sure doctors — not AI — remain responsible for determining what care patients need while bringing greater transparency to the use of these technologies in health insurance.”

“When a computer system is making decisions about health care, people will get hurt,” said Landsman. “We have to make sure health care professionals remain the decision makers. If not, folks will be left with massive bills, their health getting worse, or even life-threatening consequences.”

The Doctors Not AI Act:

Ensures AI is used only in a supporting role and requires independent clinical judgment for decisions about whether care is medically necessary;

Requires insurers to include AI-generated outputs in the administrative record, disclose the use of AI systems in the claims review process, and make the documentation available to patients; and

Promotes fair coverage for mental health treatment by preventing disproportionate algorithmic scrutiny of care for mental health and substance use disorders.

NATCHITOCHES, LA — Congressman Cleo Fields (LA-06) today announced that Northwestern State University has been awarded $1.8 million in federal funding through the U.S. Department of Commerce's National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) to support the university's Innovation Park Equipment Expansion (IPEX) Project. The funding request was submitted in collaboration with U.S. Senators Bill Cassidy and John Kennedy.

The award will allow the university to purchase cutting-edge equipment for Innovation Park, including an AI supercomputer, laser cutters, and advanced 3D printers.

“Innovation Park is a cornerstone of STEM education in Northwestern Louisiana,” said Congressman Fields. “This funding will expand research and innovation opportunities, empowering students to deepen their STEM expertise and drive groundbreaking discoveries. It will give students the critical skills they need to lead the next wave of scientific and technological innovation, and give Louisiana employers the workforce they need to grow. I was proud to work alongside Senator Cassidy and Senator Kennedy to bring these resources home to Natchitoches and to ensure Louisiana institutions get their fair share of federal investment in research and workforce development.”

The equipment is expected to expand research and innovation opportunities at Innovation Park, provide students with hands-on experience in high-demand fields, strengthen the university's ability to attract and retain top undergraduate and graduate students and faculty, and support Louisiana's broader economic development priorities in advanced technology, industrial engineering, and biomedical research.

The award was made under NIST's Congressionally-Identified Projects program (CFDA 11.617).

text:
WASHINGTON — Today, Congressman Gabe Evans’ Open-Source AI Leadership Act passed the the House Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Commerce, Manufacturing, and Trade, advancing the legislation for consideration by the full Committee.

Rep. Evans introduced the legislation to strengthen America’s leadership in open-source artificial intelligence as the United States competes with China for technological dominance — in addition to encouraging commonsense guardrails on this technology to protect consumers. The bill directs the Department of Commerce to support the adoption and use of American open AI models by identifying barriers, coordinating with American companies and startups, and developing policies that help U.S. innovation compete at home and around the world.

The legislation also takes aim at the growing national security and economic risks posed by AI models developed by foreign adversaries. It requires the Commerce Department to assess risks involving Americans’ personal and proprietary information, supply-chain security, model accuracy and censorship, safeguards against misuse, and threats involving chemical, biological, radiological, nuclear, or other national security capabilities.

If enacted, the Commerce Department will publicly report its findings and compare the adoption, cost, capabilities, and performance of foreign adversary models with qualified American open models.

“The race for AI leadership is a race America cannot afford to lose. Communist China is working every day to outcompete us, steal American innovation, and expand its technological influence around the world. We should be making it easier for our nation's innovators and startups to build, compete, and lead. This bill helps unleash American open-source AI while implementing common sense consumer protections. It also creates safeguard to identify and counter national security threats from foreign adversaries. America built the technologies that changed the world, and we’re going to keep leading.” –– Congressman Gabe Evans

The Open-Source AI Leadership Act will:

Support American open-source AI by identifying and addressing barriers that prevent U.S.-developed models from being adopted and used.

Connect government with American innovators, including startups, to strengthen adoption of U.S. open AI models.

Expose risks from foreign adversary AI, including threats to Americans’ data, cybersecurity, supply chains, national security, and economic security.

Increase transparency by requiring public assessments of leading foreign adversary AI models and comparisons with American alternatives.

The legislation defines qualified open models as those developed and made available by U.S. persons and excludes models developed or made available by covered nations or entities controlled by them.

Cincinnati, OH – Today, Congressman Greg Landsman (D-OH-01), Congressman Buddy Carter (R-GA-01), Congresswoman Kim Schrier (D-WA-08), and Congressman Tom Barrett (R-MI-07) introduced bipartisan legislation to prevent artificial intelligence from making health care decisions that should be made by qualified health care professionals.

Health care systems are increasingly using artificial intelligence (AI) to evaluate claims and determine if certain health care for patients is “medical necessity. This has led to denials of claims – impacting mental health coverage, cancer treatment, hospital stays, and more.

In response, Representatives Landsman, Carter, Schrier, and Barrett introduced the bipartisan Doctors Not AI Act – legislation to ensure medical decisions are made by a health professional, not AI.

The Doctor’s Not AI Act would:

1. Ensure AI is only used in a Supporting Role

Prevents AI from making or issuing harmful determinations involving medical judgment.

Allows insurers to use AI technology to assist with processing claims.

Requires that denials based on medical necessity be made by a licensed health care professional with appropriate expertise.

2. Protect Independent Clinical Judgment

Requires health professionals to independently review each patient’s individual medical circumstances.

3. Increase Transparency

Requires disclosure when AI is used in the review process and must be included in the administrative record.

Gives patients the right to know if AI has played a role in their insurance denial.

4. Protects Access to Mental Health Care

Helps prevent AI from unfairly denying or limiting mental health and substance use disorder care.

Congressman Landsman:

“When a computer system is making decisions about health care, people will get hurt. We have to make sure health care professionals remain the decision makers.If not, folks will be left with massive bills, their health getting worse, or even life-threatening consequences.”

Congressman Carter:

“Every patient’s medical needs are unique and decisions about their care require the judgment of a qualified health care professional, not an algorithm. While AI can help make the claims process more efficient, it should never have the final say in denying someone access to medically necessary care. I am proud to co-lead the Doctors Not AI Act to put patients first, preserve independent clinical judgment, and bring greater transparency and accountability to insurers’ use of AI.”

Congressman Schrier, M.D.:

“It is critical that doctors, not automated systems or AI-powered models, are in charge of critical healthcare decisions for their patients. We are now seeing insurers implement automated systems that can make dangerous decisions about a patient’s health, coverage, and treatment plans. Medical decisions should be made by health professionals, and we need oversight and transparency now to keep Americans safe and healthy.”

Congressman Barrett:

“Artificial intelligence should never replace the judgment of a doctor. When it comes to someone’s health and well-being, the outcome is too important to leave it up to an algorithm. This bill makes sure doctors — not AI — remain responsible for determining what care patients need while bringing greater transparency to the use of these technologies in health insurance.”

Craig Obey, Senior Vice President of Federal Affairs at Inseparable

“Insurance coverage decisions that affect someone’s mental healthcare, cancer treatment, or hospital stay should never be dictated by an algorithm. AI should be used responsibly and only as a supplementary tool, not substitute for the informed judgment of trained clinicians about the care patients need. The DNAI Act will ensure that patients are protected through a more transparent, fair, and honest system.”

text:
Congresswoman Dina Titus today applauded a decision by the Interior Department’s Board of Land Appeals to halt development of a data center on federal land adjacent to Boulder City.

“The judge ruled for transparency and public accountability in granting a stay based on the BLM’s misuse of an environmental impact statement for a solar farm as justification for a data center. The two are vastly different.” Congresswoman Titus said. “I’ve said since day one that this was not only improper but illegal.”

Congresswoman Titus was the first public official to criticize BLM's rubber stamp of approval, sending a letter to the BLM in early July stating, “Residents of Boulder City and other communities in Southern Nevada have a right to know about any proposal to transfer federal land to data center developers. Data centers potentially can affect our scant water resources, energy usage, and the overall environment. The BLM allowed a private developer to switch from developing a solar farm on city-owned land in Boulder City to building a data center on adjacent federal land without any public review. This is unacceptable.”

Boulder City and several environmental groups filed an appeal with the Interior Department’s Board of Land Appeals. The proposed data center project would be the first data center built on BLM land, setting a precedent for how data center decisions will proceed across Nevada and the Western United States. There are currently 76 built or planned data centers in the Silver State.

Administrative Judge David Gunter wrote in granting the stay, "Appellants have made a persuasive showing that BLM violated NEPA and acted arbitrarily or capriciously when it determined that the data center project is 'substantially the same' as the solar plant project for purposes of its NEPA analysis."
